entry.title: Memory Is Understood Backward: Anthropic’s Agent-Memory Components, Checked Against My Claude Code Setup

link.title: Memory Is Understood Backward: Anthropic’s Agent-Memory Components, Checked Against My Claude Code Setup

entry.content:
On November 6, 2026, Anthropic published The components of agent memory, and a Chinese translation went round on X a few days later. It opens with Kierkegaard: life can only be understood backward, but it must be lived forward. An agent has the same problem with memory. It writes notes in the middle of a task, before it knows which details will matter later.

I use Claude Code every working day, with a memory stack I built one piece at a time: raw session transcripts, a search index over tool output, a size-capped notes index, and a local Hindsight daemon. The article gave me a chance to check that stack against Anthropic’s own experiments. This post summarises the article, maps my layers onto it, and lists the gaps it made me see. The mapping is my analogy, not Anthropic’s.

What the article says

The article defines agent memory as knowledge Claude gains from experience and keeps between sessions, saved as context it can read later. It excludes three neighbours: changes to weights, in-context learning within one conversation, and compaction.

It then separates two components:

Component When What it does Cost
Memory notes During the task Claude writes notes to a store (a folder of files, a database) Takes attention from the main task; sees only the current session
Dreaming Between sessions Claude rereads logs and transcripts to fix mistakes and build new notes and representations Needs compute; its output is not available immediately

Dreaming builds on the idea of sleep-time compute from researchers at Letta and UC Berkeley: use idle time between interactions to reorganise what you already have.

The experiments behind it:

  1. Strong models choose what to remember better than fixed rules do. About 10,000 steps into Pokémon, Sonnet 3.7 had written 413 memory files across 225 folders and earned one badge. Fable 5 had nine files in two folders plus one global.md, and four badges. At one point Sonnet 3.7 spent 17 steps creating six files and deleting nine without taking a single action in the game.
  2. Steering helps older models; rules can hurt newer ones. On a CL-Bench 1.0 database task, telling Sonnet 4.6 to read its memory before answering and to test its theories nearly doubled its score. Sonnet 5 read its memory first 9 times out of 10 without being told. When Opus 5 and Opus 4.7 were told to “record only failures”, they lost much of the gain memory had given them.
  3. A transcript gives dreaming a ground truth to check notes against. In Mt. Moon, Claude had noted the wrong side of the mountain for a landmark and walked off a one-way ledge. A dreaming pass checked the note against the transcript, rewrote it, and with the corrected note Claude went straight back into the cave.
  4. Wikis help with cross-document questions and can also bloat. On merger questions that needed several documents, Claude scored 87% from a wiki it had built against 73% from search alone. On a task where a single text search found the answer, the wiki added nothing clear. On another, the wiki grew larger than the documents, like the map in Borges’s story that is as large as the empire.
  5. Dreaming can promote notes. It can float notes to the top of the memory hierarchy, where the harness loads them at the start of every session, so Claude does not need to know there is something to search for.
  6. Dreaming fills gaps one session leaves. A second pass found nine wiki links to a missing page, repointed them to the existing page for the same document, and added three pages, including an index.

The open questions at the end: when to write memory (in the moment distracts; in the background is late), and how to keep it current, perhaps by aiming dreaming at information that is likely to change or tuning its cadence by how often memories are accessed. The article also calls it reasonable to treat transcript search as the foundation that other representations sit on.

My stack, layer by layer

Layer Tool What it holds How it gets read
Raw transcripts Claude Code session files + find-session.py Every prompt, tool result and reply Regex search, on demand
Working set context-mode ctx_search Large tool output, fetched pages, indexed docs, a journal of the session BM25 search, on demand
Curated notes Auto-memory files + MEMORY.md One fact per file, with why and how to apply it Index preloaded every session; files read on demand
Always-loaded rules ~/.claude/rules/*.md Facts promoted from one project to all of them Preloaded in every project
Long-term store Hindsight, one bank per repo Retained transcripts, deliberate documents, mirrored notes, generated pages Pages injected on the first prompt; recall, document get and reflect on demand

find-session.py: the transcript as ground truth

find-session.py is a short Python script of mine that searches Claude Code’s session transcripts with a regex. By default it searches only the prompts I typed. Injected instructions, memory text, subagent hand-backs and compaction summaries are skipped, because they appear in every session and would match everything. --deep widens the search to every transcript line, including tool results and Claude’s replies. --all searches every project instead of the current one. Each hit prints the last activity time, the session id, and the command to reopen it. It reads Codex CLI sessions too: their rollout files under ~/.codex/sessions/ record the working directory and mark which user messages were typed, so the same rules apply, and those hits are tagged [codex] with a codex resume command. --memories also greps Codex’s own memory files, line by line.

find-session.py 'review again' --all       # sessions where I typed it, newest first
find-session.py 'some error text' --deep   # also tool results and replies

This is the article’s foundation layer. Semantic recall is good at “what was that about”; a regex over transcripts is exhaustive for “where did I see this exact string”, and it is the record that a note can be checked against.

ctx_search: keeping output out of the context

The context-mode plugin indexes tool output that is too large to paste back. Its README describes the mechanics: output over 4,096 bytes goes into a per-project SQLite database whole, and the agent gets only the best-matching chunks plus a pointer for the rest. Each chunk lands in two FTS5 tables, one word-stemmed and one trigram. ctx_search ranks each table with BM25 and fuses the two lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion. A search can cover the current session, the worktree (the default), or the whole project. After compaction, ctx_resume gives back a small state block.

By the article’s definition most of this is not memory. It is context management, close to compaction, which the article excludes. It earns its place differently: a 50 KB log never enters the conversation, and I can query it ten minutes later without running the command again.

MEMORY.md: notes promoted by hand, with a hard cap

Claude Code’s auto-memory writes notes to Markdown files in a per-project folder. The format I use keeps one fact per file, with a type (user, feedback, project, reference) and, for feedback, a Why and a How to apply line. MEMORY.md is the index: one line per memory. Claude Code’s documentation says the first 200 lines or 25 KB of it, whichever comes first, load at the start of every conversation, and the rest does not.

Today my index for one busy repo is 125 lines and about 18 KB, pointing at 204 memory files. A SessionStart hook of mine warns when the index reaches 80% of either limit. Closed items move to an ARCHIVE.md that does not load. A memory that matters in every project gets promoted again, out of the project and into ~/.claude/rules/, which loads everywhere.

This is the article’s “top of the memory hierarchy”, with one difference: nothing promotes my notes automatically. I do it, or Claude does it when I ask.

Hindsight: retain, recall, pages, reflect

Hindsight runs as a local daemon with one memory bank per repository. These are the operations I use:

  • Retain, automatic. The coding-agent plugin writes each session’s transcript into the repo’s bank when Claude stops.
  • Retain, deliberate. A durable finding or an external document goes in under a fixed document id. To update it, I retain the full new text under the same id, then read it back with document get and compare it with the source before trusting it.
  • Mirror. A sync script (hindsight-sync-memory.py) copies my auto-memory files into the same bank, one document per section, and re-retains only what changed. Hooks run it in the background at session end, and on Stop at most once every ten minutes, because a long-lived session can go days without ending.
  • Pages. Hindsight keeps a set of generated pages per bank, a curated digest of the memory behind them. I set the plugin’s autoInject to pages, so the first prompt of a session gets the page passages that match it.
  • Recall. Semantic search that returns extracted facts, not the stored text. It is good for “why did we decide this”. It is bad for exact values, because table cells and literal strings get lost in extraction, so exact values come from document get.
  • Reflect. An LLM synthesis over the bank. In my setup it runs on an open-weights model through a router (see my consolidation settings). On November 6 I stopped relying on its answers: once it drew only on the current session and proposed a change that ran against the purpose of the design I had asked about. I read stored memory instead, through pages, recall and document get, and check each fact against its source.

The split between the two stores is deliberate. MEMORY.md holds only what must reach every session: hard rules, feedback that changes behaviour, and one-line pointers. Reference data, dates, recipes, history and closed items go to Hindsight, which has no load limit. Moving an item means writing it to Hindsight, reading it back, and only then trimming the note to a pointer.

Where the article and my setup agree

Judgement over rules. The “record only failures” result matches how my notes are written. Many of them start from a mistake, but each one is written as a rule plus its reason, not as a log of what went wrong. The reason lets the model handle the case the rule did not foresee.

Check the note against the record. The article uses the transcript to correct a wrong note. The Hindsight plugin’s injected guide says the same thing about everything it surfaces: what it returns is “a past record, not a live reading”. A note that says “fixed” or “version X is deployed” is what someone said then. I re-read the code or the live system before acting on it.

Volatile facts. The article suggests aiming dreaming at information that is likely to change. My answer so far is to not store volatile values at all. Where a fact changes weekly, such as what version is deployed where, the memory holds the command that fetches it, not the value. A pointer to a command cannot go stale the way a copied value does.

Borges’s map. The article’s oversized wiki is why I like a hard cap on the always-loaded tier. 200 lines force abstraction: one line per entry, details one link away. Hindsight has no such cap, which is one more reason I read exact values from stored documents and not from a synthesis.

Where I differ: no automatic dreaming

My settings.json has autoDreamEnabled: false. I could not find that setting in Claude Code’s public documentation, so I describe only my reason for it. A background pass that merges and deletes entries on its own judgement is exactly the process most likely to misjudge a rare hard rule, and a wrong deletion is silent. The article names the related costs: notes can be wrong from the start or drift, dreaming to fix them requires compute, and maintained representations have to be kept from accumulating errors or hallucinations.

So my consolidation happens in two supervised places. When the size hook warns, I tidy MEMORY.md with Claude and read the diff. Hindsight builds its pages in a separate store, where nothing it does can delete a note I wrote. Promotion is manual all the way up: project note, then index line, then global rule. It is slower than dreaming, and a person has read every promoted line.

Gaps the article showed me

  • Nothing fills cross-session gaps. The article’s second dreaming pass fixed nine broken wiki links. My notes link to each other with [[name]], and a link to a note not yet written is allowed on purpose, as a marker of something worth writing. Nothing ever sweeps those links. A read-only check that lists dangling links and index lines whose file is gone would get the benefit of that pass without the risk of automatic deletion.
  • Writing in the moment has a cost. My notes are written mid-task, which the article says distracts from the task. I accept that for now, because the notes I most need are corrections, and those are clearest at the moment they happen.
  • Synthesis is the weakest layer. The article’s wiki works because Claude both builds and checks it. My generated pages and reflect answers are useful leads, but until I can check them against their sources as cheaply as a note against a transcript, they stay leads.

References

  • Lance Martin, Anthropic, The components of agent memory, November 6, 2026.
  • 刘老板 (@leo_xiaolei), Chinese translation of the article on X, November 10, 2026.
  • Lin et al., Sleep-time Compute: Beyond Inference Scaling at Test-time, Letta and UC Berkeley, 2025.
  • Claude Code documentation, How Claude remembers your project.
  • context-mode README, “How it works” section.
  • My earlier posts: a local Hindsight daemon for Claude Code and Codex, Hindsight consolidation settings, and choosing long-term memory for Hermes.
entry.summary: Anthropic splits agent memory into notes written in the moment and dreaming done afterward. What its experiments found, how my stack of transcripts, ctx_search, MEMORY.md and Hindsight lines up with it, and why I still keep automatic consolidation off.

entry.title: Why I Removed RTK from Claude Code: Reading JetBrains’ Paired Benchmark

link.title: Why I Removed RTK from Claude Code: Reading JetBrains’ Paired Benchmark

entry.content:
Until July 2026 I ran RTK v0.39.0 (“Rust Token Killer”) in Claude Code. It is a CLI proxy: a PreToolUse hook rewrites shell commands such as git status into rtk git status, RTK runs the real command, and the model receives a compressed version of the output. The pitch was 60–90% fewer tokens.

On July 20, 2026, JetBrains published a paired A/B benchmark of RTK. On July 22 I removed it: the hook, the instruction file it adds, and the binary. This post explains why I think the benchmark is right, where it is limited, and what my own session data says.

Scope. This is a commentary, not a new benchmark. The JetBrains numbers are theirs. My own numbers come from 247 Claude Code session transcripts on my machine (September–November 2026), recorded after RTK was gone, so they estimate what RTK could touch if I reinstalled it today. They are not a before/after comparison.

1. What JetBrains measured

The article is part 2 of a series that runs the same paired benchmark against public “token saving” add-ons for coding agents. Part 1 tested the caveman skill (advertised −65%, measured −8.5%).

   
Agent Claude Code 2.1.201, headless, pinned in both arms
Model claude-sonnet-5, full run at low and at high reasoning effort
Benchmark SkillsBench, 86 of 87 tasks, auto-graded with partial credit
Treatment RTK v0.43.0 exactly as rtk init -g ships it: binary, PreToolUse hook, RTK.md
Volume 425 billed trials, about USD 320

The results:

  Low effort High effort
Median per-task cost change with RTK +7.6% (p=0.004) +0.1% (p=0.99)
Turns +13.8% (p=0.03) +0.0 (p=0.74)
Task quality (better / worse / tie) 5 / 4 / 71 5 / 4 / 62

So RTK did not hurt quality, and at no effort level did it save money. At low effort it cost slightly more: more turns, more cache reads. Pairs where the hook rewrote many commands cost about 24% more than baseline; pairs it barely touched cost about 5% more.

What I value in the method is that it measured the bill, paired by task, with the endpoints fixed before any paid run. It also kept RTK’s own audit log for every trial, so “RTK saved nothing” can be told apart from “RTK never ran.”

2. Why the advertised saving had nowhere to live

The compression itself is real. git status turned into three lines and pytest reduced to its failures look great in a demo. The article’s point is that the demo measures the wrong thing. Three mechanisms do most of the work.

The hook sees only a fraction of the context. Claude Code reads files with its built-in Read tool and searches with Grep. Neither goes through the Bash hook; RTK’s own README says so: “The hook only fires on Bash tool calls. Built-in tools like Read, Grep and Glob do not pass through it.” Of the Bash calls left, JetBrains found that many are python3 … and other commands RTK has no filter for, or heredocs and substitutions that RTK deliberately does not rewrite. In JetBrains’ replay of 83 baseline transcripts, the commands RTK could rewrite carried just under 20% of tool-result characters. Compress all of that by 70%, and the ceiling is about 3% of input tokens.

Claude Code already truncates the pathological cases. RTK’s scoreboard (rtk gain) counts the full raw output as what it saved. One cat of a 1.2 MB CSV logged 320k tokens “saved”, but Claude Code truncates a tool result long before that size, so the model would have received a few thousand tokens either way.

Most of the input bill is cached re-reads. Every turn re-reads the whole context from the prompt cache, billed at a tenth of the normal input price. RTK estimates tokens as characters ÷ 4 at the moment the command runs, which says nothing about how that output is billed afterwards.

Put together, RTK’s scoreboard reported 96.2 million tokens saved during the low-effort run, while the measured bill for the same trials went up.

3. Checking it against my own sessions

My workflow is more shell-heavy than a benchmark agent’s. I tell the agent to filter output at the source (grep, head, jq) and to keep Read for files it is about to edit. So I checked whether RTK’s ceiling is higher for me. I replayed the transcripts and attributed every tool result to the tool that produced it:

Share of all tool-result characters My sessions
Bash, any command 66.2%
Bash, without a heredoc, command substitution or file redirect 42.3%
Bash, and the command contains one RTK has a filter for 33.8% (upper bound)

That last line is generous. It counts the whole output of grep … | head -20 as compressible, although head already cut it. Even so, RTK could reach about a third of my tool output, against just under a fifth in the benchmark.

Then the dilution starts. In the same transcripts, tool results were roughly 10% of the tokens written into the prompt cache. Cache reads were 98% of all input tokens. A third of a tenth is about 3% of what enters the context. Compressing it by 70% gives roughly 2–3%. My workload is more exposed to RTK than SkillsBench, and the ceiling still lands where JetBrains put it.

Two caveats. Tokens here are characters ÷ 4, like RTK’s own estimate. The replay covers main sessions only, not subagent transcripts.

4. Where the article stops

  • One model, one benchmark. claude-sonnet-5 on SkillsBench. The full 86-task runs were one attempt per task (k=1) at each effort level.
  • One RTK version. The benchmark tested v0.43.0 (June 28, 2026) in hook mode. RTK v1.0.0 (October 13, 2026) added pipelines and an rtk-proxy daemon that works on the provider-API traffic itself; v1.1.0 (October 25) is the current release. Neither benchmark nor I tested that, and I would not extrapolate in either direction.
  • The README is more careful now. On July 22, 2026, two days after the article, RTK added a “How Savings Work” section that scopes its numbers to bash output: “it is not the same as cutting your bill by the same amount.” The header still promises compression “up to 90% smaller”, now explicitly about bash output.

None of these change my decision. The structural argument, a filter on a fifth to a third of tool output inside a bill dominated by cached re-reads, does not depend on the model or the version.

5. What I use instead

I kept one layer: the context-mode plugin. Instead of compressing output after the fact, it runs a command or script in a sandbox and returns only what the script prints. A 2,000-line test log becomes “3 failed: …” because the script asked that question, not because a filter guessed what mattered.

I have not run a paired benchmark on it either. The lesson from this article applies to it as much as to RTK, and that is the main thing I took away:

A tool’s self-reported savings are a claim about its counterfactual, not about your bill.

If you are evaluating any context-compression tool for a coding agent, run the same tasks with and without it, pair them, and compare the invoices. Its own dashboard cannot tell you that.
entry.summary: RTK advertised 60–90% fewer tokens; a paired benchmark measured a 7.6% cost increase at low effort and no change at high effort. A commentary on why the saving had nowhere to live, checked against my own Claude Code sessions.

entry.title: Adding a Mic Button to a Web App: Five Ways to Build Voice Input, and Why a Server Relay Wins

link.title: Adding a Mic Button to a Web App: Five Ways to Build Voice Input, and Why a Server Relay Wins

entry.content:
A mic button next to a chat box looks like a small feature. The user taps it, speaks, sees the words appear in the input, edits them if needed, and presses send. Nothing is spoken back. This is dictation: speech-to-text (STT) feeding an ordinary text field.

It is much simpler than a realtime voice conversation, where the assistant answers aloud, either side can interrupt, and turn-taking has to feel natural. Dictation needs none of that. It still raises one architectural question that is easy to get wrong: where does the audio go, and who controls the connection to the recognizer?

“Pick an online STT provider” answers only half of that. The provider decides recognition quality. The architecture decides latency, browser coverage, billing, abuse protection, and how painful it is to switch providers next year.

This article compares five ways to build it and explains why a backend WebSocket relay is the default I would pick for a product.

Scope. This is an architecture comparison, not a benchmark. Browser and vendor capabilities were checked against official documentation on November 4, 2026; latency notes are qualitative unless stated otherwise.

1. What actually decides the choice

Before comparing options, fix the requirements. For a dictation box in a product, these are the ones that separate the options:

Requirement Why it matters for dictation
Live partial results Words should appear while the user is still talking. Waiting until they stop feels broken.
Recognition quality Mixed languages, product names, and domain vocabulary are where recognizers differ most.
Browser coverage A mic button that silently does nothing in one browser is a support ticket.
Cost and metering Commercial STT is billed by audio time. If you pay per second, you probably want to meter per second.
Provider portability STT quality moves fast. You will likely want to switch providers or models at least once.
Credential safety A provider API key can never ship to the browser.
Privacy Audio leaves the device in every cloud option; the question is to whom, and under which terms.

2. Option A: the browser’s built-in Web Speech API

The browser exposes SpeechRecognition (prefixed webkitSpeechRecognition in some engines). You start it, receive interim and final results, and write them into the text field. No API key, no backend, no bill.

const Recognition = window.SpeechRecognition || window.webkitSpeechRecognition;
if (!Recognition) hideMicButton();          // unsupported browser

const rec = new Recognition();
rec.lang = "en-US";
rec.interimResults = true;
rec.continuous = true;
rec.onresult = (e) => {
  let interim = "", final = "";
  for (const r of e.results) (r.isFinal ? (final += r[0].transcript) : (interim += r[0].transcript));
  renderDraft(final, interim);              // commit final text, show interim in grey
};
rec.start();

What you get. Streaming results with almost no code, at zero marginal cost to you. For everyday speech in a major language, quality in Chrome and Safari is usually good enough for a text box the user can edit.

What you give up.

  • Coverage. Chrome and Edge support it (unprefixed since version 139, prefixed long before that). Safari supports the prefixed webkitSpeechRecognition since 14.1 on macOS and 14.5 on iOS. Release Firefox has not supported it; MDN’s compatibility data lists support arriving in Firefox 160, scheduled for November 10, 2026. Feature-detect and hide the button where it is missing.
  • Control. You cannot choose the model, and the same sentence is recognized by a different engine in each browser. Vocabulary control is limited: SpeechGrammarList is deprecated and has no effect on recognition services. Chrome 142 added SpeechRecognition.phrases for contextual biasing, but Safari has no equivalent.
  • Where the audio goes. According to MDN, Chrome’s recognition is server-based: audio is sent to a web service, so it does not work offline. Chrome 139 added an on-device path (processLocally, with available() and install()), but it is opt-in and needs a downloaded language pack. The recognition terms are the browser vendor’s, not a contract you signed.
  • No SLA. The recognizer is a browser feature, not a commercial API. Behavior can change with a browser release, and session limits are not under your control. In practice sessions also end on their own after a stretch of silence; MDN documents no limit, so handle onend and restart if you need long dictation.

When to pick it. Free dictation where “good enough in Chrome and Safari” is acceptable and you hide the button elsewhere. It is also a sensible stopgap while you build something better.

3. Option B: record, upload, transcribe

Capture audio with MediaRecorder, upload the file when the user stops, and let your backend call a batch transcription API.

This is the easiest server-side integration and it gives you full control: the key stays on the server, you meter exact durations, and switching providers is a backend deploy.

For dictation it has one disqualifying property: nothing appears until the user stops talking, and then they wait for upload plus transcription. A ten-second utterance can take several more seconds to show up. Users read that silence as “it didn’t hear me” and start over.

Batch transcription is the right tool for voice memos, uploaded recordings, and meeting notes. It is the wrong tool for a text box where the user is watching the cursor.

That leaves streaming. There are three ways to stream audio to a recognizer from a web page.

4. Option C1: the browser streams directly to the provider

Your backend mints a short-lived, single-use token; the browser opens the provider’s realtime WebSocket (or WebRTC session) with it and streams audio directly. Several STT vendors document exactly this pattern for client-side apps. For example, ElevenLabs issues single-use realtime_scribe tokens that expire after 15 minutes; OpenAI’s Realtime API issues ephemeral client secrets (10 minutes by default) that also cover transcription-only sessions; Deepgram’s grant endpoint issues JWTs with a 30-second default TTL.

Browser ──(1) POST /stt-token──► Your backend ──► Provider: mint short-lived token
Browser ──(2) WebSocket + token ─────────────────► Provider realtime STT
Browser ◄─(3) partial / final transcripts ───────── Provider

Strengths. Lowest latency (one network hop), no long-lived connections on your servers, and the smallest amount of backend code: one token endpoint.

Weaknesses. Once the token is issued, the session belongs to the client.

  1. Provider lock-in moves into your client. The provider’s URL, message format, and parameters live in front-end code. Switching providers means a front-end release. For a web app that is a deploy; for the mobile builds of the same product it is a store release and a long tail of old clients still talking to the old provider.
  2. Metering is approximate. Your server knows a token was issued, not how many seconds were streamed. To charge per second you must trust the client’s report or reconcile against the vendor’s usage data afterward.
  3. Abuse surface. A token can be extracted and used outside your app. Single-use and short expiry limit the damage, but the mint endpoint needs authentication and rate limiting.
  4. Domain logic is duplicated. Vocabulary hints, language settings, and fallback rules end up written in the client, separately from any server-side voice features you already have.
  5. No server-side observability or fallback. If the provider degrades, the server never sees it and cannot fail over.
  6. Content Security Policy. The provider’s WebSocket origin must be allowed in connect-src.

When to pick it. Dictation is free (or billed per use, not per second), you do not expect to change providers soon, and latency matters more than control.

5. Option C2: a backend WebSocket relay

The browser streams audio to your WebSocket endpoint. Your server authenticates the user, opens the upstream connection to the provider with the key it holds, forwards audio up and transcripts down, and meters the session.

Browser ──PCM frames──► Your relay ──PCM frames──► Provider realtime STT
Browser ◄──transcripts── Your relay ◄──transcripts── Provider
                          │
                          └─ auth · vocabulary · metering · caps · logs · fallback

Strengths.

  • Provider choice is a server setting. Switching vendors, models, or parameters is a backend deploy. Every client, including old mobile builds, moves at once.
  • Exact, server-authoritative metering. The relay sees every audio frame. Seconds of audio are bytes / (sample_rate × bytes_per_sample), measured on your side, so per-second billing does not depend on the client.
  • Enforced limits. Maximum session length, concurrent sessions per user, and balance checks happen in one place, before the provider is billed.
  • Shared domain logic. Vocabulary hints and language defaults live next to the rest of your backend instead of being re-implemented in each client.
  • Observability and fallback. Error rates and time-to-first-word are visible in server logs, and the relay can retry or switch to a secondary provider.

Weaknesses.

  • One extra hop. Typically tens of milliseconds within the same region, which users do not perceive in a stream of partial words. Put the relay near the provider’s region.
  • Long-lived connections on your servers. Each dictation session holds a WebSocket open for its duration. On a request-based platform, that connection occupies capacity for the whole time. On Google Cloud Run, for example, WebSockets are treated as long-running HTTP requests: they are subject to the instance’s concurrency limit and are closed at the request timeout (5 minutes by default, 60 at most), so clients must handle reconnects. Dictation sessions are short (seconds to a minute or two), which keeps this manageable; set a hard cap anyway.
  • More code than C1. You own the relay, its backpressure, and its error mapping.

6. Option C3: a WebRTC room with a server-side agent

Use a realtime media platform (LiveKit, or a similar SFU) the way realtime voice assistants do. The browser publishes its microphone track to a room; a server-side agent subscribes, runs STT, and sends transcripts back over a data channel.

Strengths. WebRTC runs over UDP with congestion control and loss recovery designed for live audio, so it degrades more gracefully on lossy mobile networks than a TCP WebSocket. If you already run a voice agent, its STT configuration, fallback chain, and usage accounting can be reused.

Weaknesses. It is the heaviest option for the smallest feature: a room, an agent dispatch, and a worker per session, plus the platform’s per-minute charges on top of STT. Joining a room and dispatching an agent adds start-up delay before the first word.

It is a common misconception that this option produces better recognition. It does not. All three streaming options can use the same STT model, and the model determines accuracy. What C3 adds is a more resilient transport and reuse of an existing voice pipeline. Server-side control, the property most people actually want, is equally available in C2.

When to pick it. Users dictate long passages on poor mobile networks or in noisy places, or you already operate a WebRTC voice agent and want one pipeline for both features.

7. Side-by-side

  A. Web Speech API B. Record + upload C1. Direct to provider C2. Backend relay C3. WebRTC + agent
Partial results while speaking Yes No Yes Yes Yes
Recognition quality Browser vendor’s Your choice Your choice Your choice Your choice
Consistent across browsers No Yes Yes Yes Yes
Backend code None Upload endpoint Token endpoint WebSocket relay Room + agent worker
Switch provider without client release n/a Yes No Yes Yes
Server-authoritative metering n/a Yes No Yes Yes
Server-side vocabulary and fallback No Yes No Yes Yes
Extra latency None Seconds Lowest One hop Room join + agent
Packet-loss resilience Browser-managed n/a TCP TCP UDP / WebRTC
Marginal cost Free to you STT STT STT + relay capacity STT + media platform + worker

8. Why the relay is my default

For a product, three things tend to be true at once:

  1. The recognizer will change. Especially outside English, the best realtime STT model a year from now is unlikely to be the one you start with. C2 makes that a server change.
  2. Dictation costs money per second, so it eventually gets metered. Even if it is free today, a relay lets you add limits or pricing later without trusting the client.
  3. Server-side control is what matters, not the transport. Vocabulary hints, caps, logging, and fallback are the features that improve over time, and they all live on the server in C2.

C1 is a good choice only when the first two are false. C3 is a good choice only when transport resilience is a real requirement or a WebRTC agent already exists. Option A remains a useful free tier or stopgap, with the button hidden where it is unsupported.

9. Building the relay: a minimal shape

The sketch below shows the moving parts; the provider client is an interface you implement against your vendor’s realtime API.

Client: capture 16 kHz mono PCM and stream it.

// pcm-worklet.js — runs on the audio thread
class PcmWorklet extends AudioWorkletProcessor {
  process([input]) {
    const ch = input[0];
    if (ch) {
      const pcm = new Int16Array(ch.length);
      for (let i = 0; i < ch.length; i++) pcm[i] = Math.max(-1, Math.min(1, ch[i])) * 0x7fff;
      this.port.postMessage(pcm.buffer, [pcm.buffer]);
    }
    return true;
  }
}
registerProcessor("pcm-worklet", PcmWorklet);

const stream = await navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({
  audio: { echoCancellation: true, noiseSuppression: true, channelCount: 1 },
});
const ctx = new AudioContext({ sampleRate: 16000 });   // resample in the worklet if unsupported
await ctx.audioWorklet.addModule("/pcm-worklet.js");
const node = new AudioWorkletNode(ctx, "pcm-worklet");
ctx.createMediaStreamSource(stream).connect(node);

const ws = new WebSocket("wss://api.example.com/ws/dictation");
ws.binaryType = "arraybuffer";
ws.onopen = async () => ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "start", token: await getIdToken(), lang: "auto" }));
node.port.onmessage = (e) => ws.readyState === 1 && ws.send(e.data);
ws.onmessage = (e) => {
  const msg = JSON.parse(e.data);
  if (msg.type === "partial") showInterim(msg.text);
  if (msg.type === "final") commitText(msg.text);
};

Browsers cannot set an Authorization header on a WebSocket, so the token travels in the first message. A subprotocol or a short-lived ticket in the query string also works; avoid long-lived credentials in URLs, which end up in logs.

Server: authenticate, meter, forward (FastAPI sketch).

SAMPLE_RATE, BYTES_PER_SAMPLE = 16_000, 2
MAX_SECONDS = 120

@app.websocket("/ws/dictation")
async def dictation(ws: WebSocket):
    await ws.accept()
    start = await asyncio.wait_for(ws.receive_json(), timeout=5)
    user = await verify_id_token(start["token"])          # never trust a client-sent user id
    session = await meter.open(user, max_seconds=MAX_SECONDS)

    async with stt.connect(language=start.get("lang"), vocabulary=vocab_for(user)) as upstream:
        async def audio_up():
            async for frame in ws.iter_bytes():
                session.add_seconds(len(frame) / (SAMPLE_RATE * BYTES_PER_SAMPLE))
                if session.over_limit():
                    break
                await upstream.send_audio(frame)
            await upstream.finish()

        async def text_down():
            async for event in upstream.events():         # partial / final
                await ws.send_json({"type": event.kind, "text": event.text})

        try:
            await asyncio.gather(audio_up(), text_down())
        finally:
            await session.close()                          # write usage once, server-side

10. Details that bite in production

  • Insert at the cursor, not at the end. Users dictate into the middle of a draft. Track the selection when recording starts and replace the interim span, not the whole field.
  • Interim text is not committed text. Render it differently and replace it on every update; only final segments are appended.
  • Cap the session on the server. A forgotten tab with an open microphone is billed audio. Combine a hard maximum with a silence timeout.
  • Pick one audio format and resample once. Most realtime STT APIs want 16-bit PCM at a fixed sample rate. MediaRecorder gives you Opus in WebM or MP4 containers, which many realtime endpoints do not accept.
  • Permissions and secure contexts. getUserMedia requires HTTPS (or localhost), and mobile Safari only starts audio capture after a user gesture.
  • Close cleanly. Send an explicit end-of-audio message upstream so the provider flushes the last words; otherwise the final few hundred milliseconds are often lost.
  • Disclose where audio goes. Every cloud option sends voice to a third party. Say so in the privacy policy, including for the browser’s built-in recognizer.

Summary

  • Dictation is STT into a text box, not a voice conversation. Keep it that simple.
  • Batch upload is wrong for a live text box: no words appear until the user stops.
  • The browser’s Web Speech API is free and streaming, but gives you no control and incomplete browser coverage.
  • Among streaming options, the model decides accuracy; the architecture decides control. A direct connection is fastest and simplest; a WebRTC agent is the most resilient transport; a backend WebSocket relay gives server-authoritative metering, provider portability, and shared domain logic at the cost of one hop and some connection capacity.
  • For most products, start with the relay.
entry.summary: A practical comparison of browser speech recognition, record-and-upload, direct provider streaming, a backend WebSocket relay, and a WebRTC agent for dictation in web apps, with the reasons a relay is the default.

entry.title: A Portable Voice Stack: How Lumina Tarot Connects LiveKit, STT, Any LLM, and TTS

link.title: A Portable Voice Stack: How Lumina Tarot Connects LiveKit, STT, Any LLM, and TTS

entry.content:
Lumina Tarot has a spoken follow-up conversation attached to an existing reading. The user talks naturally, the assistant replies aloud, either person can interrupt, and the conversation remains available as text afterward. The useful engineering result is a voice layer that another application can reuse: LiveKit carries audio; separate providers recognize speech and synthesize replies; the application’s own language model and business logic generate the answer.

For our general persona, that language model is DeepSeek through OpenRouter. It is not embedded in the speech stack. We can change the recognizer, the voice, or the model integration independently, subject to the conversation’s consistency rules.

This guide explains the implementation, the order in which to reproduce it, and two alternatives: an OpenAI stack informed by the open-source Codex voice implementation, and xAI’s Grok voice stack. The central advantage of the modular approach is independent control over language quality, domain behavior, and cost. Lower total cost is an optimization opportunity, not a result that follows automatically from choosing a cheaper text model.

Evidence and scope. Implementation details below come from a static review of Lumina’s private repository at commit 6392ec75f18c393eb5dda832e43190b2d7d4079e. External APIs and prices were checked against official sources on November 3, 2026. This review did not rerun production voice calls, benchmark the three alternatives, or audit current provider invoices. Examples marked as assembly sketches or pseudocode require the application-owned components described alongside them; they are not a complete downloadable application. The guide includes those contracts so a second project can implement them without access to Lumina’s repository.

1. The architecture to copy

There are two server entry points in one Python codebase:

  • FastAPI authenticates users, authorizes the domain context, quotes a session, issues a room token, and exposes authoritative status and termination APIs.
  • A LiveKit Agents worker joins the room and runs the streaming STT → LLM → TTS conversation. It imports the same domain core used by the text API.

The Flutter client sends audio to LiveKit Cloud and plays the agent’s remote audio track. It also receives transcripts, agent state, and billing snapshots. Audio is not uploaded to the REST API one recorded utterance at a time.

The distinction matters. REST is the control plane; LiveKit is the media plane. Firestore is the durable authority for account/session state and canonical conversation history. A room event is useful for a responsive UI, but it is not the final billing record or the explanation for why the server ended a session.

In this implementation, LiveKit Cloud hosts the media service while our application hosts the agent worker. Those are separate deployment choices. LiveKit documents self-hosted agent deployments as well as managed hosting; using its SDK does not require putting our business logic inside a proprietary assistant product.

2. The actual stack, including fallbacks

This is the repository configuration reviewed for this article, rather than a claim that each item is the newest available model:

Responsibility Lumina implementation Migration seam
Client Flutter, livekit_client declared as ^2.11.0, permission_handler Keep an application-owned room interface around the SDK
Media transport LiveKit Cloud rooms and WebRTC audio tracks Managed or self-hosted transport, independently of the LLM
Conversation orchestration livekit-agents==1.6.10 One orchestrator owns turn-taking and cancellation
Voice activity detection Silero VAD, prewarmed per worker process Tune against real pauses and false interruptions
Primary STT ElevenLabs scribe_v2_realtime Streaming recognizer plugin
Fallback STT Cartesia ink-whisper A separately tested language/configuration path
Domain LLM Shared application gateway through OpenRouter Chat Completions Same domain core and conversation model as text
General persona model deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash Model belongs to persona configuration
Primary TTS Cartesia sonic-3, persona-specific voice ID Streaming synthesis plugin
Fallback TTS Fish Audio plugin, latency_mode="low" App does not explicitly pin its model/voice in this constructor
Identity and storage Firebase Auth and Firestore Replaceable auth/store adapters; keep authorization semantics
API hosting Cloud Run Request-serving process
Voice worker hosting Repository’s current runbook: VPS + systemd Long-running worker, independently released and verified

The Cartesia, ElevenLabs, Fish Audio, and Silero LiveKit plugins are also pinned to 1.6.10 in the reviewed Python dependency file. Python’s minimum is 3.12. Keep a lockfile in the destination project; copying a caret range from Flutter is not the same as copying the resolved dependency graph.

The provider integration references are ElevenLabs STT, Cartesia TTS, and Fish Audio TTS. Provider docs evolve independently of the pinned application. For example, Cartesia now publishes a Sonic 3 → 3.5 migration guide; that is a reason to evaluate an upgrade, not evidence that Lumina already runs it.

Which APIs are involved?

Connection API or protocol Credential owner
Flutter → application Authenticated HTTPS REST under /api/v1/voice User identity token
Flutter ↔ LiveKit Room signaling plus WebRTC media/data Short-lived room-scoped token from our API
Worker ↔ LiveKit Agents registration, job assignment, room participation Worker-side LiveKit credentials
Worker → ElevenLabs Realtime STT WebSocket, wss://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/speech-to-text/realtime Server-side ElevenLabs key
Worker → Cartesia/Fish Audio Streaming synthesis/recognition via provider plugins Server-side provider keys
Domain gateway → OpenRouter POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions, streamed text Server-side OpenRouter key
API/worker → Firestore Firebase Admin / Google Cloud server SDK Service identity with limited permissions

Use the plugin to handle provider audio framing and connection behavior unless a measured requirement justifies a custom adapter. ElevenLabs’ realtime API reference is the relevant contract for the deployed recognizer; a batch transcription endpoint with a similar model name is not a substitute.

3. Keep domain intelligence outside the voice framework

The most important module is not a speech plugin. It is the shared domain core.

In a tarot app it supplies the reading, source evidence, persona, conversation history, language preference, and context budget. In another project it might supply a lesson, support case, order, or document. These are adapters around the same invariant:

Changing input/output modality must not silently change the facts, permissions, or model responsible for the domain answer.

A useful destination layout is:

app/
  core/
    context.py          # domain evidence, history, language, budget
    prompts.py          # persona and response policy
    llm.py              # streaming model gateway and usage
    pricing.py          # pure authorization/billing arithmetic
  api/
    voice.py            # quote/start/status/end
  voice/
    entrypoint.py       # LiveKit job and provider assembly
    domain_llm.py       # framework LLM interface -> core
    transcripts.py      # durable final/interrupted turns
    meter.py            # server authority and termination
  repositories/
    conversations.py
    voice_sessions.py

Both entry points import core. The voice worker does not loop back through the public text endpoint to obtain an answer. Lumina makes this a deliberate boundary: the public endpoint has its own transport, billing, and retry semantics, which should not become a second voice pipeline. Another application can use an internal domain service instead of a Python import, but then it must preserve the same versioned context/model contract.

Model selection is flexible; an active conversation is stable

Lumina calls its persona configuration a soul. It combines the prompt, model, voice, context budget, reasoning policy, and price. A different persona can intentionally use a different model. An existing conversation, however, records its model identity. A voice session must agree with it.

That separates three changes people often conflate:

  1. Routing the same model through another compatible upstream host: an availability decision.
  2. Selecting another model for a new persona/conversation: an explicit product/configuration decision.
  3. Replacing the model halfway through an existing conversation: a consistency change that needs a migration or a new conversation, not an invisible retry.

The general persona’s current model is DeepSeek. Other personas have their own configurations. It would be inaccurate to describe the whole application as permanently tied to one DeepSeek model.

4. Reproduce the control-plane lifecycle first

Lumina starts voice from an existing, authorized interpretation. A destination app should replace that eligibility check with its own domain rule rather than copying tarot identifiers into its storage model.

Quote → consent → start → connect

The public operations are:

Operation Endpoint Important behavior
Quote GET /api/v1/voice/quote Domain eligibility, availability, price, balance, processing disclosure
Start POST /api/v1/voice/sessions Revalidate quote; create pending record; issue room grant; return 201
Recover status GET /api/v1/voice/sessions/{id} Authoritative state, billing revision, balance, and end reason
End DELETE /api/v1/voice/sessions/{id} Idempotent termination/settlement; return 204

For a daily reading, quote query parameters include readingKind=cotd, date, and drawId. A spread uses readingKind=spread and spreadReadingId instead. Do not accept a mixture of both locator shapes.

The start request echoes the revisions the user saw in the quote:

{
  "readingKind": "cotd",
  "date": "2026-11-03",
  "drawId": "example-draw-id",
  "runtimeRevision": 7,
  "pricingRevision": "example-pricing-revision"
}

These values are illustrative. The real values come from the quote, not a client constant. The response grants a particular session and room:

{
  "voiceSessionId": "example-session-id",
  "roomName": "voice-example-session-id",
  "token": "<short-lived-room-token>",
  "livekitUrl": "wss://<your-livekit-project-host>",
  "keyterms": ["example domain term"],
  "soulId": "general",
  "blockSeconds": 12,
  "creditsPerBlock": 1,
  "creditsPerMinute": 5,
  "pricingRevision": "example-pricing-revision",
  "runtimeRevision": 7
}

The server authenticates the user, checks ownership, re-quotes against current availability/pricing, and rejects stale revisions. It transactionally enforces one pending/active voice session per account. It persists pending before returning the token. If token creation fails, cleanup releases the orphaned pending record. The current token lifetime is 300 seconds and the grant is restricted to the room and user identity; token expiry is an admission boundary, not a substitute for ending an already-connected call.

The API’s error contract includes:

HTTP Code Client response
402 INSUFFICIENT_CREDITS Offer the application’s purchase/top-up route
409 VOICE_QUOTE_STALE Fetch and present a fresh quote
409 VOICE_SESSION_ALREADY_ACTIVE Recover/end the existing session
404 INTERPRETATION_NOT_READY Return to domain eligibility flow
503 VOICE_UNAVAILABLE Preserve the conversation and allow retry/text mode

Starting a pending session does not itself spend credits. The worker validates the stored session and context, starts provider/session machinery, then authorizes the first billing block before allowing user input. Never charge merely because the client requested a token.

Client responsibilities

The Flutter room wrapper calls room.connect(grant.livekitUrl, grant.token) and then localParticipant.setMicrophoneEnabled(true). It owns mute/unmute and disconnect cleanup. The controller coordinates permission, quote display, connection, and account changes.

Keep platform microphone permission and audio-session setup in the client. Use the platform/SDK’s appropriate capture and playback processing, including echo cancellation; verify it on the actual output route rather than claiming a particular SDK default is universally sufficient. STT, TTS, end-of-turn decisions, and model generation stay on the server.

The useful UI states are connecting, listening, thinking, speaking, reconnecting, and terminal ended/failure states. Lumina reads agent state from lk.agent.state, uses LiveKit transcription events for captions, and listens for reliable data messages with topic billing_state. Account identity and a controller generation counter guard asynchronous callbacks so a previous account/session cannot update the next one.

On disconnect, call the status endpoint. A WebRTC disconnect does not tell the client whether the business reason was idle timeout, exhausted credit, provider failure, or worker shutdown. After termination, refresh canonical history with bounded retry: the worker may still be draining its final transcript write.

5. Assemble the streaming worker

The following is an assembly sketch using the reviewed SDK shape. domain_llm, the frozen persona, settings, and the prewarmed VAD are application-owned inputs; the next section defines the adapter contract. It intentionally leaves out session authorization, event wiring, and persistence so those responsibilities remain visible rather than hidden in a misleading demo.

from livekit.agents import AgentSession
from livekit.agents.stt import FallbackAdapter as SttFallbackAdapter
from livekit.agents.tts import FallbackAdapter as TtsFallbackAdapter
from livekit.plugins import cartesia, elevenlabs, fishaudio


def build_voice_session(settings, persona, domain_llm, vad, context_hint):
    return AgentSession(
        vad=vad,
        turn_handling={
            "endpointing": {"min_delay": 0.3},
            "interruption": {"mode": "vad", "min_duration": 0.25},
        },
        stt=SttFallbackAdapter(stt=[
            elevenlabs.STT(
                api_key=settings.elevenlabs_api_key,
                model="scribe_v2_realtime",
                previous_text=context_hint,
                server_vad={
                    "vad_silence_threshold_secs": 0.6,
                    "min_silence_duration_ms": 600,
                    "min_speech_duration_ms": 250,
                    "vad_threshold": 0.4,
                },
            ),
            cartesia.STT(
                api_key=settings.cartesia_api_key,
                model="ink-whisper",
            ),
        ]),
        llm=domain_llm,
        tts=TtsFallbackAdapter(tts=[
            cartesia.TTS(
                api_key=settings.cartesia_api_key,
                model="sonic-3",
                voice=persona.tts_voice,
            ),
            fishaudio.TTS(
                api_key=settings.fishaudio_api_key,
                latency_mode="low",
            ),
        ]),
    )

In Lumina, secrets are wrapped in settings types and explicitly unwrapped at assembly. The simplified example assumes strings. Load them only into server processes. The relevant environment settings are LIVEKIT_URL, LIVEKIT_API_KEY, LIVEKIT_API_SECRET, ELEVENLABS_API_KEY, CARTESIA_API_KEY, FISHAUDIO_API_KEY, and OPENROUTER_API_KEY, plus your datastore identity and domain-content configuration. Never ship those provider secrets in the mobile build.

Prewarm before a user arrives. Load Silero once in the worker’s prewarm hook and reuse it through process userdata. The repository also warms the OpenRouter connection and the TTS path. Model initialization, DNS/TCP/TLS, and an empty connection pool all otherwise land on the first audible response.

The worker entry point runs a production worker command, python -m app.agent.entrypoint start, registers with LiveKit, and handles assigned rooms. For each room it verifies the pending session and participant identity, loads the owned conversation snapshot, builds one long-lived domain LLM adapter, wires transcript/meter/shutdown events, and starts the AgentSession with the room and agent instructions. Let one orchestration framework own this lifecycle. Pipecat could replace LiveKit Agents as the orchestrator; running two competing high-level turn/cancellation loops would make behavior harder to reason about.

The domain LLM adapter is the production integration

Lumina’s VoicePinnedLlm implements LiveKit’s LLM interface. Despite its historical name, the current gateway uses an upstream provider pool rather than a fixed host chain. Its job is to:

  1. Extract the newest final user text from the framework’s chat context.
  2. Normalize only narrowly defined domain recognition errors.
  3. Resolve the account’s response language and any explicit language-switch request.
  4. Build input from the canonical domain snapshot, rolling summary, confirmed messages, and current user turn.
  5. Enforce the context budget; summarize an older complete prefix when necessary.
  6. Stream through the shared LLM gateway with the conversation’s model, converting text deltas into LiveKit ChatChunk events and usage into CompletionUsage.

A neutral version of that contract looks like this pseudocode:

async def generate_voice_turn(snapshot, final_user_text, domain_core):
    request = domain_core.prepare_turn(
        snapshot=snapshot,
        text=final_user_text,
        modality="voice",
        require_same_model=True,
    )
    # request contains canonical evidence, confirmed history, language,
    # context budget and the frozen model identity.
    async for event in domain_core.stream(
        request,
        first_content_timeout_seconds=8,
    ):
        if event.kind == "text_delta":
            yield to_livekit_chat_chunk(event.text)
        elif event.kind == "usage":
            yield to_livekit_usage(event)

Implement prepare_turn, stream, and the two conversion functions in the destination project. Keep the adapter alive for the whole voice session: rebuilding it each utterance would discard its in-memory summary and accepted history. Persistence belongs to a transcript writer, not this adapter; it should not independently charge the user or own a Firestore repository.

Voice adds a short-opening instruction to the user-turn material, leaving the persona system prompt stable. The reviewed personas configure voice reply reasoning off and reserve a maximum of 2,048 output tokens. Those are configuration choices, not universal optimal values; confirm a candidate model actually honors the relevant reasoning controls.

The current upstream routing policy is:

{
  "quantizations": ["fp8"],
  "sort": "latency",
  "allow_fallbacks": true,
  "data_collection": "deny",
  "zdr": true
}

These are OpenRouter-specific routing controls, documented in its provider routing guide. They select eligible hosts for the requested model; they do not authorize changing the model. Copy fp8 only if your chosen model has compatible endpoints. The reviewed gateway also has an 8-second first content token timeout: a connection that only emits keepalives is not useful progress. A provider routing preference cannot guarantee a response-time SLA.

6. Interruptions, transcripts, and language are one design problem

Distinguish four clocks

Voice activity, end-of-turn detection, playback, and billing have different clocks. Treating any two as equivalent causes subtle errors.

  • VAD identifies speech activity. The reviewed minimum speech duration is 250 ms.
  • Endpointing decides when a natural pause is a completed user turn. Current silence settings include 600 ms and a 0.3-second minimum endpointing delay; they are not a promise that the total delay is their arithmetic sum.
  • Interruption detection decides when user speech should stop the agent. Current mode is vad with a 0.25-second minimum duration. Shortening it can increase false interruptions.
  • Playback completion identifies what the user could actually hear. TTS finishing generation does not mean the device finished playing.

Use the current SDK’s supported configuration shape. This codebase had already moved interruption controls into turn_handling; carrying an old top-level keyword into a new SDK version can silently change behavior.

Persist the delivered answer

On a final user transcription, write the user message into the canonical conversation. Empty/whitespace input must not silently become a real turn. Partial captions can appear in the UI without becoming durable history.

For the assistant, wait for the speech/playout lifecycle rather than the synthesizer’s completion callback. If interrupted, persist the delivered prefix with interrupted status, not the unplayed generated tail. If no assistant content was delivered, abandon that pending response cleanly. Use request IDs and store-side sequencing to make retries idempotent, release the conversation lease, and avoid leaving the next turn permanently busy.

Lumina stores voice turns in the same conversation message sequence as text, marked medium=voice and linked to voiceSessionId. It does not create a second, incompatible chat-history model. This also prevents charging a voice turn a second time through the text follow-up billing path.

Evaluate the exact recognition path

The current ElevenLabs constructor passes a context hint through previous_text. That is not evidence that a special hotword API is active, nor that every recognizer honors the same biasing fields. The realtime contract and the pinned plugin’s mapping must agree. Test the actual WebSocket recognizer with real human recordings.

For Chinese, English, and mixed speech, evaluate at least proper nouns, short stop commands, domain terms, numbers, self-corrections, pauses, and code-switching. Keep recognition language, the language of source evidence, and the desired reply language separate. Lumina’s account chatLanguage preference governs replies; an explicit request to switch language can change it, while casually uttering a foreign-language word should not.

Fallback recognition needs its own evaluation. The reviewed Cartesia fallback constructor does not explicitly set a language. Do not infer Chinese parity from the primary recognizer’s results, or from a provider’s general multilingual marketing. Likewise, the Fish Audio fallback can change vocal identity because the application does not pass the Cartesia voice ID to it. Availability fallback and persona fidelity are separate acceptance criteria.

7. Meter the session on the server

Voice is billed by session authorization blocks, not by the number of generated messages. In the reviewed general persona, one credit authorizes 12 seconds, equivalent to five credits per minute. These are product credits, not provider dollars, and other persona configurations can differ.

The server freezes price/revision information when the session starts. A meter authorizes the first block and then checks on a configurable tick, currently 10 seconds. Repository transactions purchase further blocks using the expected previous authorization boundary. This makes competing ticks and repeated settlement safe against duplicate debits.

A status or billing_state message includes:

voiceSessionId, revision, startedAt, elapsedSeconds,
authorizedThroughSeconds, blockSeconds, creditsPerBlock,
creditsPerMinute, billedCredits, remainingCredits

The client discards a snapshot for another session or a non-increasing revision. It may animate an elapsed clock locally, but it does not debit credits locally. On recovery it reads the server snapshot again. A UI field called billedMinutes should not replace the authoritative block/credit fields when the actual price uses shorter blocks.

All termination routes converge on settlement: user hangup, disconnect, provider failure, exhausted credit, runtime disable, and worker shutdown. Final usage and transcript writes must be drained; stale sessions are reclaimed using the last heartbeat, not simply because a healthy call has been running for a long time.

The 90-second idle watchdog has a different purpose from billing. It pauses while the agent speaks and starts a fresh idle window when the agent stops speaking; user speech resets it. Wall-clock billing still runs. Otherwise a long answer could terminate itself because the polite listener did not interrupt. Freeze elapsed time at the termination decision where appropriate, so an explanatory closing announcement does not itself push the user into another charged block.

8. Deploy and operate the whole system

The reviewed repository describes FastAPI on Cloud Run and the voice worker on a VPS under systemd. A retained deploy_voice_worker.sh is explicitly a historical Cloud Run worker-pool/rollback reference. Do not copy an old deployment command just because the filename looks current. This article verifies the repository runbook, not a live VPS inventory.

A destination worker unit can follow this generic shape:

[Unit]
Description=Application voice agent
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
User=voice-agent
WorkingDirectory=/srv/voice-app/backend
EnvironmentFile=/etc/voice-app/worker.env
ExecStart=/srv/voice-app/backend/.venv/bin/python -m app.agent.entrypoint start
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=3
KillSignal=SIGTERM
TimeoutStopSec=120

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Provision the user, paths, virtual environment, data assets, and a root-managed environment file readable by the service. Prefer workload identity where available; if a VPS requires a service-account key, restrict its permissions and rotation surface. Do not copy project IDs, credentials, local home paths, or production room tokens from another application.

For a first destination rollout:

  1. Deploy domain/API code with new-session availability disabled.
  2. Deploy the worker from the same release, including matching prompts and domain data.
  3. Read a startup attestation: model, provider policy revision, voice, and prompt/data fingerprints; confirm worker registration.
  4. Run an authenticated room smoke test and a real device audio test.
  5. Enable availability with a compare-and-set revision; quote/start must agree on it.
  6. On rollback, disable admission first, drain or explicitly terminate existing sessions according to policy, and settle before stopping workers.

A running process or successful deploy exit is not proof of a working speech chain. Watch worker registration, assigned jobs, provider errors, time to first content token, first audible output, cancellation time, loop lag/CPU, active sessions, orphaned pending sessions, and canonical transcript write failures. Test under concurrency: a prewarmed VAD on a busy worker can behave differently from a single-user laptop demo.

Transport encryption does not mean that recognition, model, and synthesis providers cannot process the content. Keep the user-facing processor disclosure synchronized with every active primary/fallback provider. Lumina’s quote contract exposes processors and storesRawAudio; the migration should set those from a verified processing inventory. Application-side absence of raw-audio storage is not a claim that every upstream has zero retention. OpenRouter privacy routing also applies only to that LLM hop.

A read-aloud button is a different pipeline

Lumina also synthesizes already-generated reading text for playback. That path can share the Cartesia model and persona voice configuration, but it is not the realtime follow-up room. Read-aloud has text rendering, audio encoding, caching, and playback concerns; live conversation has microphone input, turn-taking, interruption, and session metering. Invalidate cached audio when text, synthesis version, model, or voice identity changes. Keep shared synthesis constants in a lightweight module rather than importing the whole worker into the API process.

9. A migration sequence that reaches a usable product

The following order avoids building a voice demo that must later be rewritten to fit the domain.

Step Build Evidence to collect before moving on
1 Shared context/model gateway Same owned domain snapshot and model identity for text and voice preparation
2 Quote/start/status/end API and store Ownership, stale revision, concurrent starts, token failure cleanup
3 One room with primary STT/LLM/TTS Real mic → final transcript → domain answer → audible playback
4 Interruptions and canonical history Interrupt before speech, mid-sentence, and near completion; no unplayed tail or stuck lease
5 Client lifecycle Permission denial, mute, Bluetooth/speaker route, reconnect, backgrounding, account switch, hangup
6 Server authorization/meter Repeated ticks, block boundary, exhausted balance, idle timeout, shutdown, stale recovery
7 Fallbacks and language matrix Deliberately break each provider; verify Chinese, English, mixed terms and voice changes
8 Staged deployment and usage reconciliation Registered worker, matched release fingerprints, final history, complete provider costs

Replace five domain-specific pieces: eligibility/ownership lookup, canonical evidence snapshot, persona/prompt policy, history/context-budget store, and product pricing. Preserve the transport/worker/client boundaries and lifecycle tests. The destination need not use Firebase, Flutter, or tarot data to keep this design.

In Lumina, useful source entry points for the owner are backend/app/agent/entrypoint.py, voice_llm.py, transcript_writer.py, meter.py, billing_publisher.py, backend/app/api/v1/endpoints/voice.py, backend/app/services/voice_session_service.py, voice_quote_service.py, backend/app/repositories/voice_session_repository.py, and lib/reading_followup/voice/. These are private implementation pointers, not prerequisites for following this guide.

Measure latency from end of user speech to first audible agent output, then split it into endpointing, final STT, context assembly, LLM first content/first speakable phrase, TTS first frame, and transport/playout. Report p50 and tail percentiles alongside sample count, language, region, load, and warm/cold state. Historical POC numbers from another provider combination are not current production benchmarks. This guide deliberately makes no universal sub-second or 1.5–2.5-second claim.

10. Alternative A: an OpenAI stack, with Codex as an architecture reference

The open-source Codex repository contains a real interactive voice implementation. For a reproducible reference, this review pinned it to commit 781d89b91e2487c3653208b9c13287e1a09f6f04.

The useful source map is:

Source What to learn from it
tui/src/app_server_session/realtime.rs TUI starts realtime with WebRTC, V3, audio output, and client-managed handoffs
realtime-webrtc/src/session.rs Local voice helper, SDP negotiation, device/mute lifecycle
core/src/realtime_conversation.rs Realtime state, transcripts, delegation, backend results
core/src/context/realtime_delegation.rs Explicit handoff from spoken conversation to background work

The architectural lesson is a responsive voice front end delegating substantive work to a backend agent. Do not equate the conversational voice model with the model executing coding tasks. At this commit, Codex’s V3 default is gpt-live-1-codex; older protocol paths retain gpt-realtime-1.5. That is not proof that a third-party app should request the Codex-specific model ID, use a ChatGPT backend endpoint, or reuse a consumer login token. Open-source client code is also not evidence that the hosted models and the entire service behind it are open source.

Public implementation: GPT-Live plus an OpenAI backend

For a new application, the closest public counterpart is GPT-Live: a full-duplex spoken conversation layer that delegates reasoning and tools. A full OpenAI implementation uses gpt-live-1 + a Responses backend model + application-authorized tools. The voice layer can listen while speaking, while the backend performs longer work. Official delegation documentation describes the separation.

Client microphone/speaker
          ↕ WebRTC
       GPT-Live
          ↕ delegation and progress/results
   OpenAI Responses backend
          ↕ authorized application tools
       Domain services

The domain backend must still own access control, durable task state, confirmation for consequential actions, and canonical records. A model-generated tool request is not authorization.

There is an important hybrid option: GPT-Live client delegation can call an application’s own model, agent, or service. It could therefore keep Lumina’s DeepSeek domain core. OpenAI is not limited to an all-OpenAI backend. What changes is control over the speech front end: STT and TTS are no longer independently selected as in our cascade. If the voice layer paraphrases a domain answer, evaluate whether that satisfies the product’s same-answer requirement. See delegation modes.

GPT-Live has its own public session API; the model page lists v1/live/sessions. Do not paste a Realtime session payload or endpoint into a GPT-Live example and assume compatibility.

A separate OpenAI option: Realtime speech-to-speech

OpenAI also offers Realtime, including gpt-realtime-2.1 and gpt-realtime-2.1-mini. This is another public speech-to-speech route, with WebRTC/WebSocket, session events, tools, and server-side controls. For client access, the application backend creates a short-lived credential via POST /v1/realtime/client_secrets; the WebRTC flow uses /v1/realtime/calls.

This is not the same API or pricing model as GPT-Live. For a destination project, choose one contract first and implement its event, interruption, credential, and tool lifecycle faithfully.

OpenAI reduces the amount of speech orchestration we own and is attractive when conversational responsiveness and rapid integration matter most. The tradeoffs are speech-provider dependence, a different cost structure, and the work needed to integrate domain consistency and history. Independent provider selection remains more granular in the Lumina cascade; backend model choice is not exclusive to it.

For new implementations, check OpenAI’s deprecation notices. The Realtime beta was removed on May 12, 2026; do not build against old beta headers. Legacy gpt-realtime/gpt-realtime-mini are scheduled for removal on January 20, 2027, and older TTS models have their own retirement schedule. Pin the intended API/model and keep a migration check in the release process.

11. Alternative B: Grok Voice through xAI

xAI’s current Speech to Speech API connects over:

wss://api.x.ai/v1/realtime?model=grok-voice-3.0

At the review date, grok-voice-latest points to 3.0 and 2.0 is deprecated. Use a fixed model for reproducible evaluation; an alias can change behavior. The native path puts the conversational speech model on xAI rather than independently selecting three vendors.

The application server obtains a short-lived client token from POST https://api.x.ai/v1/realtime/client_secrets. Its ephemeral-token guide shows expires_after.seconds, for example 300 seconds. A mobile/web client should never receive the permanent xAI API key.

The connection flow is:

  1. Authenticate the application user and authorize the domain session.
  2. Obtain a short-lived token on the backend.
  3. Connect the client or a controlled audio bridge to the WebSocket.
  4. Send session.update with instructions, a supported voice, input/output formats, turn detection, and tools.
  5. Stream audio and handle transcript/audio events; execute application functions behind server authorization.
  6. On interruption, cancel generation as appropriate and stop/clear local playback. Truncate unplayed conversation content so model history does not imply the user heard it.
  7. Reconcile final history, usage, and application session state on termination.

The voice API reference specifies cancellation/truncation events. A WebSocket gives the application direct control, but also leaves audio buffering and device playback responsibilities that a managed room/SDK may otherwise cover. For a WebRTC client, xAI publishes a WebRTC bridge example: the application-side media bridge connects to xAI over WebSocket. That should not be described as the same native WebRTC service contract as OpenAI’s endpoint.

Grok supports tools including custom functions and hosted search capabilities. Application function arguments still need validation, identity checks, write authorization, and idempotency. Tool fees can be additional to voice fees. Its documentation includes Chinese support, but support is not a measured claim about Chinese accuracy, accent handling, terminology, or mixed-language quality relative to our providers.

xAI also exposes separate STT and TTS APIs, including REST and streaming endpoints. They can be components in a custom cascade with a third-party LLM. Thus the real comparison is native Grok speech-to-speech versus an independently assembled pipeline, not an assertion that every xAI product prevents modular composition. See its voice overview, STT, and TTS documentation.

12. Compare flexibility, experience, and cost fairly

Criterion Lumina-style cascade OpenAI native voice / delegation Grok native speech-to-speech
Speech recognition Independently select and evaluate primary/fallback Managed inside the native speech layer Managed inside native Grok voice
Domain LLM Application-controlled; DeepSeek is one configuration All-OpenAI backend, or custom backend through GPT-Live delegation Grok native model; external domain computation can be reached through tools
Voice synthesis Independently select provider/voice/fallback Integrated voice layer Integrated voice layer; built-in/custom voices
Domain text parity Direct generation through shared core Must verify delegation/rephrasing behavior Must verify tool/result/rephrasing behavior
Language optimization Tune each component, including mixed-language failure cases Evaluate native speech experience as a whole Evaluate native speech experience as a whole
Interaction Framework turn detection and barge-in; more seams to tune GPT-Live offers full-duplex conversation and delegation Native session VAD, audio events, tools
Operations API + media service + worker + multiple vendor connections Less separate speech orchestration; domain backend still required Less separate speech orchestration; WebSocket media lifecycle still required
Failure recovery Fine-grained fallback and diagnostics, more states API/session-specific recovery API/session-specific recovery
Cost control Independent rates, model choice, routing, worker utilization Voice charges plus backend/tools or audio-token billing Native voice duration plus text-input/tools charges

Current public price references

These are different meters, not interchangeable per-minute totals:

Product Public price checked November 3, 2026 What else to account for
OpenAI gpt-live-1 $0.05/minute, billed per second Backend model and tools are additional
OpenAI gpt-realtime-2.1 Audio input $32 / output $64 per 1M tokens; cached audio input $0.40 Text tokens and other usage have separate rates
OpenAI gpt-realtime-2.1-mini Audio input $10 / output $20 per 1M tokens; cached audio input $0.30 Same token-versus-duration distinction
xAI Grok Voice 3.0 $0.08/minute plus $0.004 per billable text input Hosted tools may add fees; billing depends on turn mode
xAI separate STT REST $0.10/hour; streaming $0.20/hour Not the native voice-session tariff
xAI separate TTS $15 per 1M characters LLM, transport and app hosting remain separate

Sources: OpenAI pricing, GPT-Live model pricing, xAI pricing, and Grok speech-to-speech billing details. Old xAI examples quoting $0.05/minute are not the current Voice 3.0 tariff.

For xAI’s default server_vad, audio billing follows session duration, so silence matters. Push-to-talk bills audio sent and received instead.
