The text-input fee has exceptions, including function-call outputs and audio input items; do not multiply every protocol event by $0.004. Consult the billing details rather than treating all modes as identical.

To evaluate our cascade, calculate:

session cost =
    STT billed duration × recognizer rate
  + LLM input/cache/output tokens × applicable rates
  + TTS billed characters/audio × synthesizer rate
  + LiveKit transport/connection charges under the actual plan
  + allocated worker + API + storage/network cost
  + failed/retried/fallback usage not already included above

Use actual billable units, including provider-specific silence and rounding rules. Do not assume a recognizer charges only human speaking time. Fixed VPS cost divided across a nearly idle app can dominate; spare capacity on an existing VPS can make incremental hosting inexpensive, but it is not a portable zero-dollar hosting assumption.

Lumina records STT seconds and TTS characters/audio by provider, transport seconds, and LLM usage linked through voiceSessionId. A missing or incomplete usage record is unknown, not free. The reviewed cost tooling still treats some Cartesia credit-to-dollar conversions as unknown; a reported subtotal must not be presented as a verified all-in cost. Get contractual/account pricing or reconcile invoices before claiming a cost advantage.

For a deliberately narrow illustration, 10 minutes at the published GPT-Live voice rate is $0.50 before backend/tools. Ten default-VAD minutes at Grok Voice 3.0’s audio rate is $0.80 before billable text inputs/tools. Neither number is our measured product cost, and neither establishes a quality-equivalent comparison. Our cascade is cheaper for a workload only if its fully accounted total is below the competing workload’s fully accounted total. Re-evaluate after changing language mix, reply length, model, voice, provider plan, or worker utilization.

Choosing a lower-cost DeepSeek text model can reduce the LLM term substantially for an appropriate workload. It cannot by itself establish that the whole voice conversation is cheaper than every OpenAI or Grok configuration. The lasting advantage is that each term remains independently tunable.

13. Choosing a starting point for the next project

Use the Lumina pattern when the domain answer must come from a specific model or evidence pipeline, Chinese/mixed-language evaluation requires independent STT/TTS choices, or vendor-level cost and fallback control are central requirements. Budget for the lifecycle and operational work described above.

Use an OpenAI native voice layer when fast integration and conversational responsiveness matter more than independently selecting speech components. For a Codex-like assistant that works while the user keeps talking, evaluate GPT-Live delegation; a custom backend can preserve existing domain intelligence. Use the separate Realtime API when that session/model contract fits the intended application.

Use native Grok Voice when its conversational behavior, voices, tool ecosystem, and measured language quality fit the product, and its duration/text-input tariff works for the expected workload. Its separate STT/TTS APIs are also candidates for a modular design.

Whichever route you choose, retain application ownership of authorization, canonical domain context, durable history, consequential tool actions, and cost records. Those boundaries are what make voice portable across projects, even when every provider in the chain changes.
entry.summary: An implementation and migration guide to Lumina Tarot's modular voice pipeline, with session APIs, shared domain logic, interruptions, billing, deployment, and OpenAI and Grok alternatives.

entry.title: Hindsight Consolidation Settings: Low Reasoning, Batch 8, and Jev

link.title: Hindsight Consolidation Settings: Low Reasoning, Batch 8, and Jev

entry.content:
After setting up a shared Hindsight daemon for my coding agents, I ran into the next problem: the memory was being captured, but background consolidation was slow. The machine was not spending most of its time on database writes. The model calls dominated the measured processing phases.

The configuration I kept is low reasoning for consolidation, eight facts per LLM batch, and TypeSafe Jev as a decision model for one opted-in bank. The main LLM remains gpt-6-luna through Hindsight’s chatgpt provider.

This is a follow-up to my local daemon setup guide. It covers the settings and an operational tuning session on October 24, 2026, using Hindsight API 1.1.0 and coding-agents integration 0.8.2 on macOS. It is not a controlled model benchmark or proof that these settings are optimal for every bank.

Update, October 25, 2026: I later gave reflect its own LLM and Jev decision route and replaced the local reranker with a remote one. Unlike consolidation, the reflect decision model is on for every bank by default. Those changes, and two routing experiments I dropped, are in the October 25 update.

Update, October 29, 2026: The current reranker is cohere/rerank-4-fast through OpenRouter, replacing Voyage after upstream rate-limit failures. The configuration example below is updated; the October 25 measurements remain historical. See the October 29 update.

What consolidation gives me

Consolidation turns related retained facts into observations: knowledge that can be updated as evidence changes. It can reconcile repetitions, incorporate corrections, and retain references to the facts supporting an observation. The underlying facts remain available. Hindsight observations

That distinction matters for development history. A memory bank might contain both “we tried batch four” and “we restored batch eight.” The useful result is an observation that distinguishes an experiment from the current decision, with evidence for both. Simply retrieving both statements leaves that reconciliation to every later answer.

Consolidation is useful for long-lived project memory, but it is not required before raw facts can be queried. A backlog means the derived observation layer is behind; it does not by itself mean the original material was lost.

The settings I kept

Setting Effective value
Main LLM provider chatgpt
Main LLM model gpt-6-luna
Consolidation reasoning effort low
Facts per consolidation LLM batch 8
Consolidation group parallelism 4, unchanged
Memories per consolidation round 100, unchanged
Consolidation decision provider typesafe
Decision model alias jev-latest
Jev scope for consolidation One opted-in project bank

The alias resolved to jev-1.14.0 in the connectivity tests. That identifies what answered then; a moving alias is not a version pin. TypeSafe model aliases

The coding-agent configuration still uses daemon mode, an hourly page-refresh schedule, and a survey refresh after 20 commits:

{
  "serverMode": "daemon",
  "pageTriggerCron": "H * * * *",
  "surveyRefreshCommits": 20
}

Those are selected fields from the existing configuration, not a replacement for the complete file. I left the page and survey settings unchanged during these consolidation tests. They describe separate background work. Coding-agent configuration

The daemon configuration

For the coding-agent profile, the following is an explicit rendering of the effective consolidation configuration. Batch size, parallelism, and round size are shown even where the installation can inherit their defaults:

# ~/.hindsight/profiles/coding-agent.env
HINDSIGHT_API_LLM_PROVIDER=chatgpt
HINDSIGHT_API_LLM_MODEL=gpt-6-luna

# Restrict the reasoning change to consolidation.
HINDSIGHT_API_CONSOLIDATION_LLM_REASONING_EFFORT=low
HINDSIGHT_API_CONSOLIDATION_LLM_BATCH_SIZE=8
HINDSIGHT_API_CONSOLIDATION_LLM_PARALLELISM=4
HINDSIGHT_API_CONSOLIDATION_MAX_MEMORIES_PER_ROUND=100

# Give consolidation its own decision-model route.
HINDSIGHT_API_CONSOLIDATION_DECISION_MODEL_PROVIDER=typesafe
HINDSIGHT_API_CONSOLIDATION_DECISION_MODEL_MODEL=jev-latest
HINDSIGHT_API_CONSOLIDATION_DECISION_MODEL_API_KEY=YOUR_TYPESAFE_API_KEY

# Banks opt in individually below.
HINDSIGHT_API_CONSOLIDATION_USE_DECISION_MODEL=false

Replace the placeholder with the real TypeSafe key in the local profile and keep the file owner-readable only. I already had the key in JEV_API_KEY; Hindsight’s configured credential is the operation-specific variable shown above. The example contains no usable credential.

The provider, model, and credential overrides above are for consolidation only. I did not set a global decision provider, so this block by itself does not switch recall or reflect to Jev. Hindsight decision-model configuration Reflect later got its own decision-model route; see the October 25 update.

After changing the profile, restart the daemon through its normal manager and verify the new process is ready. During this session, the stop command’s short wait expired while a request was still finishing. I checked the old process had exited and the replacement was healthy before treating the restart as complete.

Opt in one bank

The profile-level false above is deliberate. It keeps other banks from using the newly configured Jev route. The selected bank overrides it to true through Hindsight’s hierarchical configuration API:

BANK_ID='coding-agent::example-repo'

curl --fail-with-body --silent --show-error \
  -X PATCH \
  "http://127.0.0.1:9077/v1/default/banks/${BANK_ID}/config" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"updates":{"consolidation_use_decision_model":true}}'

These examples assume the same loopback API without authentication used in my setup; an authenticated installation needs its configured authorization header. Verify the resolved bank configuration with GET on that same URL. Bank configuration API

In my verification, the selected bank had consolidation_use_decision_model=true, while the other three banks remained disabled for Jev. The effective batch size stayed at eight.

A bank-level setting is also subject to the operation boundary: in the observed runtime, an already-running consolidation round retained its starting configuration. Saving a new value was not proof that the current round had switched.

Why I started with low reasoning

Before this tuning session, neither the global nor the consolidation-specific reasoning effort was explicitly set. The model service chose its default; I could not label that default as low, medium, or high from the configuration alone.

I set only HINDSIGHT_API_CONSOLIDATION_LLM_REASONING_EFFORT=low. Hindsight’s performance guide recommends keeping reasoning budgets low for extraction and consolidation. Performance guidance

The first live observation improved from roughly 7.8 to 11.4 facts per minute of instrumented phase time, but the windows contained different numbers of facts and different batch distributions. I treated that as a reason to keep testing, not as a defensible claim that low reasoning alone caused a 47% speedup. The complete no-Jev baseline used below was already running with low reasoning and batch eight.

Why batch four did not stay

Smaller batches looked promising early in the run. The apparent advantage faded once the complete 100-fact round finished:

Per 100 facts Batch eight Batch four
LLM calls 30 45
Input tokens 355,223 421,962
Instrumented phase time 583.894 s 578.473 s

Here, phase time is the sum of the logged recall, LLM, embedding, and database-write phases. It excludes orchestration overhead. It is a different measure from the whole-round wall time in the Jev comparison below.

Batch four changed that phase-time throughput by only about 1%, while making 50% more LLM calls and using about 19% more input tokens. The rounds processed different facts, so a difference this small was not persuasive evidence of a speed improvement. I removed the temporary bank override and restored eight.

I also kept group parallelism at four. The installed consolidation implementation serializes batches that write to the same observation scope. Raising the concurrency ceiling would not automatically make that work parallel. Consolidation implementation

What Jev actually does here

The built-in flow is:

New facts + candidate observations + bank mission
                       |
                    Jev triage
                       |
        +--------------+----------------+
        |                               |
 Simple cases handled directly    Changes, conflicts, or
 with their supporting facts      cases needing rewriting
                                        |
                              Main consolidation LLM

Jev supplies typed judgments. The main LLM still writes the updates that need it. The installed code also checks the judgments against one another and applies the bank’s mission before accepting a shortcut. My bank has a custom mission, so the triage is deliberately conservative. Built-in triage implementation

I checked the actual requests rather than stopping at a successful configuration read. They appeared under decision_consolidation_triage, contained the new fact, candidate observations and mission, and returned successful TypeSafe responses. The early integration audit recorded no triage batch above 0.23 seconds. Over the complete test round, the logged triage batches totalled 3.73 seconds; individual request durations overlap because calls run concurrently.

The complete Jev test

Both rows below used low reasoning and batch eight. Each round processed 100 facts:

Metric Without Jev With Jev
Whole-round wall time 590.273 s 457.936 s
Facts per minute 10.16 13.10
Main LLM calls 30 25
Main LLM input tokens 355,223 297,555
Main LLM output tokens 25,014 19,373
Jev requests 0 105
Jev input tokens 0 351,929

That is an observed 28.9% throughput increase, or 22.4% less elapsed time, and 16.7% fewer main LLM calls. These are three different metrics. There were no recorded request errors, triage fallback warnings, or permanently failed facts in the Jev test.

The two rounds consumed different facts from a live backlog. This was a sequential operational comparison, not a paired A/B test. I did not run a complete semantic-quality evaluation, so the measurements do not prove that merge correctness or later answers improved. Request count is also not a unique-fact count: 105 Jev requests were recorded while processing 100 facts.

The added cost

TypeSafe’s published direct price, checked on October 24, 2026, is $0.042 per million input tokens, with output tokens free. Official models and pricing

For the recorded round:

351,929 / 1,000,000 * $0.042 = $0.014781

That is about 1.5 cents of added Jev API usage per 100 facts in this sample. Two tiny connectivity tests added approximately $0.000027. These are estimates from returned usage and the public price, not an account invoice.

The main LLM uses my existing ChatGPT plan. Fewer calls primarily save plan quota and processing time; they do not reimburse the added Jev bill. At this workload’s rate, a backlog of roughly 2,450 facts would add about $0.36 of Jev usage. Different context sizes, retries, or new incoming work change that estimate.

Update, October 25: reflect and recall

The consolidation settings above did not change. Late on October 24, running into the early hours of October 25, I turned to the interactive side, because reflect answers felt slow. One logged reflect spent 28.7 seconds in model calls and 0.22 seconds in its retrieval tools. The time was going to the remote model, not to the laptop.

These settings were added to the same profile. The reranker entry now shows the October 29 replacement; the other entries are unchanged:

Setting Effective value
Reflect LLM provider openrouter, automatic upstream routing
Reflect LLM model openai/gpt-oss-120b
Reflect reasoning effort low
Reflect decision provider typesafe
Reflect decision model alias jev-latest
Reranker provider openrouter
Reranker model cohere/rerank-4-fast 
# ~/.hindsight/profiles/coding-agent.env (additions)

# Reflect gets its own LLM route. Retain and consolidation keep the main chatgpt route.
HINDSIGHT_API_REFLECT_LLM_PROVIDER=openrouter
HINDSIGHT_API_REFLECT_LLM_MODEL=openai/gpt-oss-120b
HINDSIGHT_API_REFLECT_LLM_REASONING_EFFORT=low
HINDSIGHT_API_REFLECT_LLM_API_KEY=YOUR_OPENROUTER_API_KEY

# Reflect decision model. On for every bank unless a bank opts out.
HINDSIGHT_API_REFLECT_DECISION_MODEL_PROVIDER=typesafe
HINDSIGHT_API_REFLECT_DECISION_MODEL_MODEL=jev-latest
HINDSIGHT_API_REFLECT_DECISION_MODEL_BASE_URL=https://api.typesafe.ai
HINDSIGHT_API_REFLECT_DECISION_MODEL_API_KEY=YOUR_TYPESAFE_API_KEY

# Remote reranker through OpenRouter's rerank endpoint (updated October 29).
HINDSIGHT_API_RERANKER_PROVIDER=openrouter
HINDSIGHT_API_RERANKER_OPENROUTER_MODEL=cohere/rerank-4-fast
HINDSIGHT_API_RERANKER_OPENROUTER_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/rerank
HINDSIGHT_API_RERANKER_OPENROUTER_API_KEY=YOUR_OPENROUTER_API_KEY

The biggest operational change is not a number: reflect answers are now written by gpt-oss-120b on a pay-per-token route, not by the gpt-6-luna model on my ChatGPT plan. The reranker also sends each query and its candidate memory text to OpenRouter and the upstream reranking provider. Embeddings stay local.

Moving the reflect LLM alone was not faster

I picked gpt-oss-120b after a published leaderboard listed the Groq-served model at an average of 2.2 seconds of total reflect time. I had no Groq key, so I routed it through my existing OpenRouter key. Three complete reflects took 23.4, 30.4, and 34.0 seconds, no better than the 28.7-second example. OpenRouter was choosing the upstream provider automatically.

Pinning OpenRouter to Groq passed an authentication check, but complete reflects then failed repeatedly with tool-call validation errors. I reverted to automatic routing. The model route stayed because the next two changes were measured on it; it is not a speed improvement by itself.

Remote reranking

Recall was the other slow step. With the default local reranker, cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 on CPU, one recall over 300 candidates had a median of 4.56 seconds, and reranking alone took 4.39 of them. With OpenRouter’s cohere/rerank-v3.5, the recall median fell to 0.90 seconds and reranking to 0.72 seconds: an 80.2% reduction in recall time. That test used three repository queries, two repetitions each per provider, on the live bank. Hindsight reranker configuration

Cohere v3.5 bills by search unit, and one 300-candidate call cost four units: $0.004. I then compared reranker models alone, on a fixed set of 300 documents for each of three repository queries, two repetitions each:

Model Median time Median API-reported cost per call Successful calls
Local MiniLM-L6 on CPU 4.19 s $0 6/6
voyageai/rerank-3-lite 0.72 s $0.00105 6/6
cohere/rerank-v3.5 0.77 s $0.00400 6/6
cohere/rerank-4-fast 0.79 s $0.00800 6/6
qwen/qwen3-reranker-8b 2.37 s $0.01626 1/6, others HTTP 503

Voyage matched Cohere’s speed at about a quarter of the cost, so I switched to it. The costs are what OpenRouter reported for these calls, not list prices. Local model load time is excluded; remote times include network setup.

This is not a quality ranking. The repository queries have no labelled answers, and the models ordered the candidates differently. On a small synthetic probe with one known answer, every model that returned a result put that answer first. A recall in the live log later that day scored 300 candidates in 1.27 seconds.

The reflect decision model

The same TypeSafe Jev model can orchestrate reflect. When it is enabled, the retrieval layers run together in one round, the decision model prunes the evidence, and it judges whether that evidence already answers the question. If it does, reflect skips the main LLM’s layer-by-layer tool turns. The main LLM still writes the answer, and a decision-model error falls back to the normal agent turns. Reflect agent implementation

I compared it with the bank setting switched off and on, interleaved, at the high reflect budget: two fixed questions with two repetitions each, so four requests per side.

Per reflect Decision model off Decision model on
Median time 14.0 s 5.78 s
Median main LLM calls 5 2
Answers passing a basic check 4/4 4/4

The median fell by about 59%. One request with the decision model still took 14.8 seconds. Four requests per side is a small sample, the basic check is not a quality grade, and I did not measure the added Jev cost for reflect.

The scope differs from consolidation. Consolidation needed a bank to opt in. For reflect, the installed configuration defaults reflect_use_decision_model to true: setting up a reflect decision provider turns it on for every bank, and a bank opts out. Knowledge-page refreshes have their own switches, also on by default, and use the same reflect decision route. Configuration defaults To keep a bank off the Jev route for reflect:

BANK_ID='coding-agent::example-repo'

curl --fail-with-body --silent --show-error \
  -X PATCH \
  "http://127.0.0.1:9077/v1/default/banks/${BANK_ID}/config" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"updates":{"reflect_use_decision_model":false}}'

I left it on for all banks. In the daemon log covering the trials and the following day, 19 reflects completed through the decision model with no logged decision-model failure; two of them are the empty Cerebras answers described below. OpenRouter’s automatic routing did surface intermittent upstream provider errors. Hindsight retried them; one query-rewrite call still failed after its fourth attempt, and that reflect fell back to searching the question as written and completed.

Why Cerebras did not stay

Cerebras serves gpt-oss-120b quickly, so I also pinned the reflect route to it, with fallbacks off, keeping the Jev and Voyage settings. Three questions, two repetitions each:

Median reflect time Automatic routing Cerebras only
Short factual question A 13.0 s 2.97 s
Short factual question B 7.07 s 2.00 s
Broad summary question 36.1 s Empty answer, both runs

On a fixed prompt, Cerebras answered in 0.57 seconds against 3.74 seconds, but its mean API-reported cost per call was about 9.3 times higher: $0.00139 against $0.000148.

The empty answers decided it. The query-rewrite stage classified the summary question as needing no retrieval, and the request returned HTTP 200 with no text. A faster route that silently returns nothing for broad questions is a regression.

One operational trap: the daemon manager wrote the trial routing override into the profile, so it survived the trial. I removed it by hand and restarted. After any temporary trial, read the effective profile before trusting it.

Update, October 29: replace the rate-limited reranker

Voyage’s reranking route began returning HTTP 429. Those retrieval failures caused complete reflect requests to return HTTP 500, even though the daemon and database were healthy. I replaced voyageai/rerank-3-lite with cohere/rerank-4-fast, still using the same OpenRouter endpoint and key. OpenRouter reports Cohere as the upstream provider for the replacement. Cohere 4 Fast on OpenRouter

Before switching, I tested two fixed synthetic queries, each against 300 documents, with three repetitions per model. Each query had one independently specified correct document:

Model Successful calls Mean successful-call time API-reported cost per successful call
cohere/rerank-4-fast 6/6 0.72 s $0.006
cohere/rerank-v3.5 6/6 1.10 s $0.003
qwen/qwen3-reranker-8b 4/6; two HTTP 503s 1.86 s About $0.0078

Every successful response ranked its query’s correct document first. Both Cohere models reported three search units per call in this fixture. These costs differ from the October 25 measurements because the documents differ; 300 documents do not guarantee the same billable workload. This is a small availability and ranking check, not a general quality comparison or a sustained-load test.

I kept 4 Fast for its lower latency in this sample. After updating the profile and restarting the daemon, three simple reflect probes all returned the expected answers: 10.84, 8.88, and 6.49 seconds, averaging 8.74 seconds. Those are complete reflect times, distinct from the reranker-only times in the table. They verify recovery, not a controlled speedup against the earlier failed requests. An explicit refresh also restored a previously paused knowledge page.

How I will judge the next change

I kept Jev, low reasoning, and batch eight because this run showed a useful operational improvement at a small measured added cost. I kept Jev limited to the bank being tested.

For the next change, I want the same starting observations and fact corpus on both sides, repeated runs, full wall time including decision-model work, and a quality grade alongside cost. That grade should cover duplicates, corrections, temporal updates, and whether the bank’s mission is still being followed.

The useful outcome is a memory bank that stays current at an acceptable cost. A shorter model response or a faster first few batches is only one part of that result.

The measurement summary includes the configuration, counters, timing definitions, and limitations used for the calculations in this post, including the October 25 comparisons and the October 29 reranker replacement.
entry.summary: The Hindsight configuration I kept after testing: low-reasoning consolidation with Jev triage for one bank, then a remote reranker and a Jev-orchestrated reflect, with measured costs and limitations.

entry.title: Choosing Long-Term Memory for Hermes: 10 Options, Trade-offs, and Cloud Pricing

link.title: Choosing Long-Term Memory for Hermes: 10 Options, Trade-offs, and Cloud Pricing

entry.content:
Choosing Long-Term Memory for an AI agent starts with a practical question: what should the agent remember, and how will you know that it remembered correctly?

Hermes offers several approaches: curated Markdown files, a local fact database, user-modeling services, knowledge graphs, and directory-based context stores. They solve different problems and charge for different units of work.

This guide compares 10 options, including Hermes’s built-in memory, with their strengths, trade-offs, integration paths, and cloud pricing. The pricing snapshot is dated October 23, 2026. All amounts are in US dollars. Annual commitments and annualized monthly prices are labeled explicitly.

This is a documentation-based comparison, not a hands-on benchmark using identical tasks. Vendor accuracy scores use different models, datasets, and cost assumptions, so they are not treated as a common leaderboard.

Start with the memory you actually need

Persistent memory can mean several things:

  • Personal facts and preferences: time zone, communication style, and long-term goals.
  • Project decisions and lessons: architectural choices, debugging findings, and working conventions.
  • History and change: when a preference changed or why a decision was revised.
  • External knowledge: documents, websites, email, and shared team material.

A small preference store and a traceable engineering knowledge base need different systems. Write down the questions you want the agent to answer before choosing the backend.

The 10 options at a glance

Option Main use Deployment Cloud entry point
Hermes built-in memory Curated facts, preferences, conversation lookup Local No separate memory-service fee
Honcho User modeling and reasoning-based recall Cloud or open-source self-hosting $2 per million ingestion tokens; reasoning extra
OpenViking Directory-based knowledge and tiered loading Cloud or self-hosted Managed service advertises the first 50 files free; exact usage rates require confirmation
Mem0 Automatic fact extraction and maintenance Cloud, self-hosted server, or OSS Free; Starter $19/month
Hindsight Relationships, time, and synthesis across memories Cloud or open-source self-hosting Prepaid usage
Holographic Lightweight local fact storage Local No additional model calls by default
RetainDB Managed memory, hybrid search, and files Cloud Free; Builder $9/month
ByteRover Project knowledge and team synchronization; distinguish legacy provider from V4 skill Local-first, optional cloud sync Current cloud plans: free; Pro $15/month billed annually
Supermemory User memory, document retrieval, and connectors Cloud or licensed local server Free; Pro $19/month
Memori Tool-aware memory and production governance OSS or managed deployments Free allowance; production Team from $60,000/year

Hermes allows one active external memory provider at a time, while built-in memory remains active. Additional MCP tools can coexist, but that does not automatically give them another provider’s background synchronization and recall lifecycle. Hermes integration documentation

1. Hermes built-in memory

Hermes stores curated facts and preferences in MEMORY.md and USER.md. Its session_search tool can retrieve earlier conversations. Official documentation

Pros

  • Human-readable files are easy to inspect, edit, back up, and migrate.
  • No additional memory account, API key, or service dependency is required.
  • It provides a straightforward baseline for stable project conventions and personal facts.
  • It remains available alongside an external provider.

Cons

  • Resident memory is bounded and needs curation as information accumulates.
  • Files alone do not provide sophisticated relationship modeling or fact reconciliation.
  • Sharing memory with other coding tools requires an additional integration.
  • Historical recall still depends on the agent choosing useful queries.

Pricing: There is no separate SaaS fee. Injected memories still occupy the main model’s context and incur its normal token costs.

Best fit: Start here when a small set of stable facts and searchable conversation history may already solve the problem.

2. Honcho

Honcho focuses on understanding users over time. It maintains representations of users and agents and offers reasoning at several depths. It has a dedicated Hermes integration and an open-source core.

Pros

  • A good architectural match for persistent preferences, goals, and user modeling.
  • Ordinary context retrieval is separate from deeper reasoning.
  • Multiple tools can connect to a shared memory layer.
  • Self-hosting gives control over the infrastructure and stored memory.

Cons

  • Inferred user attributes require review; they are not equivalent to explicitly confirmed facts.
  • Frequent deep reasoning can dominate the bill.
  • Refresh frequency and reasoning depth need deliberate configuration.
  • Self-hosting transfers model provisioning and operations to you.

Cloud pricing

Operation Published rate
Ingestion and processing $2 per million input tokens
Context retrieval Listed as unlimited
Background Dreaming Included
Minimal reasoning $0.001/query
Low reasoning $0.01/query
Medium reasoning $0.05/query
High reasoning $0.10/query
Max reasoning $0.50/query

The current personal-memory page states that new accounts receive $5 in credits, with another $5 each billing period after adding a payment method. Recurring credits do not accumulate. This uses the live page rather than older cached signup offers. Rates, credit terms

Unlimited context retrieval does not eliminate the main agent’s cost of reading that context.

Best fit: A personal assistant that should maintain a coherent understanding of the same user across sessions and tools.

3. OpenViking

OpenViking organizes context as a virtual filesystem under viking://. Agents can browse directories and load L0 abstracts, L1 overviews, and L2 source content progressively.

Pros

  • The knowledge structure is visible and navigable.
  • Project or directory scope can narrow retrieval.
  • Summary-first loading helps control how much material reaches the agent.
  • Archived sessions and extracted Markdown memories can be inspected.

Cons

  • Self-hosting requires running a service and configuring its models, adding operational work.
  • Generated summaries and retrieval planning can introduce errors.
  • Directory design may be unnecessary overhead for a small preference store.
  • Product capabilities and the subset exposed by the Hermes integration should be evaluated separately.

Cloud pricing: OpenViking offers a managed service on Volcengine alongside self-hosting. Its enterprise page advertises the first 50 files free and hourly pay-as-you-go; exact usage rates should be checked in the service console. Self-managed enterprise deployment is custom-priced. Self-hosting costs depend on compute, storage, embeddings, and the configured language or multimodal models. Deployment options, enterprise offering

Best fit: Larger, clearly structured knowledge collections where inspecting and maintaining the organization matters. Website, Hermes integration

4. Mem0

Mem0 offers automatic fact extraction and memory CRUD operations, with a managed platform and an open-source implementation.

Pros

  • A direct API for adding user-level memory to an existing agent.
  • Cloud, self-hosted, and in-process OSS deployment choices.
  • Explicit free and entry-level quotas make an initial trial easier to budget.
  • Pro adds graph memory and Dream consolidation.

Cons

  • Extraction can omit context or preserve inaccurate or outdated information, so extracted memories still need review.
  • Lower tiers provide substantially fewer retrieval requests than add requests.
  • Per-turn retrieval can exhaust the retrieval quota first.
  • Pro represents a substantial price increase; its capabilities should not be assumed to exist in Starter.
  • OSS deployments leave you responsible for the configured models and storage; defaults are provided and can be overridden.

Cloud pricing

Plan Monthly price Add requests/month Retrieval requests/month Projects
Hobby $0 10,000 1,000 1
Starter $19 50,000 5,000 1
Pro $249 500,000 50,000 Unlimited
Enterprise Custom Listed as unlimited Listed as unlimited Unlimited

Pro includes graph memory, Dream, analytics, and private Slack support. Enterprise adds features such as SLA support, on-premises deployment, audit logs, and SSO. Current pricing

Best fit: Managed fact extraction with a simple API, provided that the retrieval quota matches the intended agent loop.

5. Hindsight

Hindsight separates retain, recall, and reflect: storing information, retrieving it, and synthesizing answers across memories. It also models entities, relationships, temporal changes, and mental models. Open-source project

Pros

  • A strong architectural match for questions about how a project or decision evolved.
  • Explicit operations distinguish retrieval from synthesis.
  • Cloud includes memory-side LLM, embedding, and reranking models.
  • An upstream-maintained Hermes integration is available.

Cons

  • Capturing full conversations and tool calls can increase ingestion volume.
  • Reflection, model refreshes, and long-term storage have separate meters.
  • Automatically refreshed knowledge pages can generate charges without a manual refresh.
  • Self-hosting requires operating databases, models, and upgrades.
  • Synthesized conclusions still need supporting evidence.

Cloud pricing

Operation Rate
Retain $10 per million input tokens
Import or restore from an export archive $5 per million input tokens; no new fact extraction
Recall $0.75 per million output tokens
Reflect $0.05/call
Retrieve Model or read a knowledge page $0.25 per million output tokens
Refresh Model or create/update a knowledge page $0.05/call
Iris enhanced file extraction $7.50 per million output tokens, plus normal retain
Memory storage after 30 days $0.25 per million tokens/month, accrued daily

Cloud uses prepaid credits at $1 per credit. The homepage advertises $5 in initial credits for GitHub signup; this is not a recurring monthly allowance. Standard text extraction avoids the additional Iris charge, but retaining extracted content still costs money. Billing details, what Cloud includes

Best fit: Projects that need temporal context, entity relationships, and synthesis across multiple memories.

6. Holographic

Holographic is a local SQLite fact store combining FTS5, entity resolution, trust scoring, and holographic reduced representation retrieval. The current plugin is maintained by a community maintainer.

Pros

  • No API key, network access, or additional model calls by default.
  • Fact versions, provenance, and correction operations support inspection.
  • Hermes backup integration and SQLite-aware backups support local recovery.
  • Optional embedding-based semantic search can use a remote API or a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

Cons

  • Keyword and HRR retrieval should not be equated with general language-model semantic understanding.
  • Large paraphrases, implicit relationships, and complex synthesis need practical evaluation.
  • Fact organization and keywords affect recall quality.
  • Remote embeddings change the data flow and may add provider charges; local embedding endpoints can keep the processing local.
  • Community-maintained compatibility is worth monitoring.

Pricing: The default local path has no separate memory-model service bill. Optional remote embeddings follow the chosen provider’s pricing; local embedding endpoints need not incur an API fee. Main-agent tokens remain separate. No managed-service quote was confirmed in this review. Current capabilities, Hermes catalog

Best fit: A modest local store of preferences, facts, and explicit decisions with minimal additional infrastructure.

7. RetainDB

RetainDB combines managed memory, hybrid retrieval, file operations, and project features.

Pros

  • Writes and context reads have separate, visible quotas.
  • The entry paid tier is inexpensive.
  • Memory, file knowledge, and collaboration can live in one service.
  • Higher plans add delta compression and larger team limits.

Cons

  • The standard route depends on a hosted service.
  • Delta Compression is not included in every tier.
  • The Hermes documentation identifies its standalone provider repository as needing a maintainer. That is an integration-maintenance issue, not a claim that the RetainDB service is unmaintained.
  • Older documentation and current pricing can differ.

Cloud pricing

Plan Monthly price Writes/month Context reads/month Scope
Starter Free $0 20,000 5,000 1 project, 1 API key
Builder $9 75,000 15,000 3 projects, 5 keys, 3 seats, Knowledge Graph
Pro $29 250,000 75,000 10 projects, 20 keys, 10 seats, Delta Compression
Scale $99 1,000,000 300,000 Unlimited projects and keys, 50 seats
Enterprise Custom Listed as unlimited Listed as unlimited Contract-specific

The pricing page also advertises 20% off annual billing. Older Hermes material lists $20/month; this table uses the current vendor pricing page. Overage behavior should be checked at checkout. Pricing, Hermes maintenance note

Best fit: Budget-conscious managed workloads with substantial read/write quotas, after checking Hermes integration compatibility.

8. ByteRover

Hermes’s documented ByteRover provider uses the legacy brv CLI and a local hierarchical knowledge tree. Current ByteRover V4 documentation instead describes Desktop, spaces, and a published agent skill; its setup guide removes the old Hermes provider before V4 setup. Both routes target project decisions, debugging lessons, and reusable engineering knowledge, but their integration details should be evaluated separately. V4 overview, agent setup and migration

Pros

  • Knowledge is readable and maintainable.
  • Selected material can be shared across devices and teams.
  • Recall sources can be inspected.
  • The legacy Hermes provider documents extraction before context compression discards insights.

Cons

  • Duplicate and outdated knowledge still needs curation.
  • The legacy provider’s LLM-driven search adds processing and can add model cost, depending on configuration.
  • The legacy CLI and the current Desktop/skill route each require client setup and synchronization management.
  • Hermes lists the standalone provider repository as needing a maintainer; the product and integration have distinct maintenance considerations.

Cloud pricing

Plan Price Main scope
Legacy local provider Listed as free in Hermes documentation Local tree; model costs depend on configuration
Free cloud sync $0 100 context files, device sync, team sharing
Pro $15/month billed annually Unlimited context files, priority support
Enterprise Custom SSO/SAML, RBAC, on-premises options

The cloud rows describe the current ByteRover offering, not an entitlement guarantee for the legacy Hermes provider. The accessible current page explicitly labels $15 as billed yearly. This review did not reliably confirm Pro’s monthly-billing price or the seat-billing basis. Older retrieval-based price tables should not be substituted for the current file-based plans. Current pricing, Hermes documentation

Best fit: Coding agents that should share inspectable project knowledge with selective team synchronization.

9. Supermemory

Supermemory combines personal memory with SuperRAG document retrieval and connectors for external sources. Its Hermes plugin is maintained by the vendor.

Pros

  • One integration ecosystem can cover personal memory and external knowledge.
  • Supported updates under the same customId within the same organization bill only newly added content on the token-ingestion meter.
  • Connectors can reduce the work of ingesting documents and cloud sources.
  • A local server is available for single-machine workflows.

Cons

  • Credits, Memory tokens, SuperRAG tokens, queries, and operations are separate meters.
  • Document identity changes or full replacements can incur fresh ingestion charges.
  • Advanced PDF extraction and some connectors require higher plans.
  • The current local server binary comes from a non-public codebase and is free only within its lite license limit. Open-source SDKs do not make the complete server open source.
  • Local extraction models and available integrations differ from the hosted service.

Cloud plans

Plan Monthly subscription Monthly included credits Main differences
Free $0 $5 APIs, plugins, 1 seat
Pro $19 $20 Auto top-up, 3 seats
Max $100 $130 More credits, Gmail connector
Scale $399 $600 Advanced PDF, S3, crawler, unlimited seats
Enterprise Custom Contract-specific Dedicated support and deployment options

Usage rates

Meter Rate
Memory plain text $5 per million SM tokens
Memory rich content $10 per million SM tokens
SuperRAG text $1 per million SM tokens
SuperRAG images, PDFs, audio, and video $2 per million SM tokens
Search and traversal $5 per million queries
Operations $100 per million operations

Subscription credits reset monthly; purchased top-up credits do not expire. An auto-top-up purchase limit is not a hard cap on the total invoice. Workflows can use multiple meters, so budget against the endpoints actually called. Plans and rates

The local server needs your extraction model. Its default embedding model is English-oriented, so multilingual workloads should evaluate alternatives. The reviewed licensing pages did not specify a numerical lite limit; it should not be described as unlimited free usage. Local deployment, Local versus Enterprise

Best fit: Workloads combining memory with documents, websites, or cloud connectors, with room for more detailed usage accounting.

10. Memori

Memori emphasizes execution traces, structured recall, and production governance. Hermes uses an externally supplied hermes-memori CLI/provider integration.

Pros

  • Tool-aware memory fits production agent workflows.
  • Production plans include access control, audit logging, observability, and memory pooling.
  • Deployment choices cover managed multi-tenant, managed single-tenant, customer VPC, and on-premises arrangements.
  • Free Cloud and OSS routes allow smaller initial experiments.

Cons

  • Paid production plans are priced primarily for enterprises.
  • OSS, free Cloud, and production contracts are different offers.
  • Counts of memories created or recalled are not directly comparable to another provider’s API-request quotas.
  • Free Cloud has monthly creation and recall limits; production plans are a separate purchase.

Cloud pricing

Plan Published price Scope
OSS Software free Bring your database, models, and infrastructure
Cloud Free $0 5,000 memories created/month; 15,000 memories recalled/month
Team From $60,000/year One production agent, managed multi-tenant
Business From $150,000/year Multiple production agents, managed single-tenant
Enterprise Custom Customer VPC or on-premises, dedicated infrastructure

Team and Business annualize to $5,000 and $12,500 per month respectively. Those are annual-contract equivalents, not published monthly purchase prices. Production plans list unlimited memories, but agent and deployment scope still differ. The Cloud FAQ and dashboard document the free allowances as monthly. Pricing, Cloud FAQ, Hermes integration

Best fit: Organizations buying production governance and vendor support rather than a low-cost personal memory subscription.

Budget for the whole memory loop

The memory provider’s price is only part of the bill.

Main-agent tokens: A free or inexpensive recall operation can still return a large context that the main model must process.

Background work: Extraction, reconciliation, reasoning, refreshes, and consolidation may run behind a simple interaction.

Operations and migration: Self-hosting requires backups, upgrades, model configuration, and troubleshooting. Changing a service URL does not necessarily migrate stored memories.

A useful budget is:

Total cost = memory subscription or metered usage
           + extraction, retrieval, and embedding costs not included
           + main-agent tokens used to read recalled context
           + self-hosted infrastructure and maintenance

Requests, tokens, synchronized files, and generated memories measure different things. One conversation is not necessarily one billable operation.

A practical shortlist

These are architectural matches, not measured performance rankings.

Primary requirement Start by comparing
Minimal maintenance Hermes built-in memory
Lightweight local facts Holographic
Inspectable project knowledge shared across tools ByteRover
Simple managed fact API Mem0
Long-term user understanding Honcho
Temporal context and synthesis across memories Hindsight
Navigable, directory-based knowledge OpenViking
Memory plus documents and connectors Supermemory
Low entry price with substantial hosted quotas RetainDB, with integration validation
Production governance and vendor delivery Memori and relevant enterprise offerings

Keep built-in memory as a common baseline. Ask each candidate the same questions: did an old preference update correctly, can a decision be traced to its source, does information leak between projects, and does a deleted memory reappear?

Record ingestion, retrieval, background operations, and main-model tokens for a complete session. That connects recall behavior to cost and gives a more useful decision than a cross-vendor accuracy chart.

Snapshot limitations: Pricing and features were checked on October 23, 2026. ByteRover’s monthly-billing price, Supermemory’s numerical lite limit, and OpenViking’s exact managed-service usage rates were not confirmed. Check the linked official documentation and checkout pages before purchasing or deploying.
entry.summary: Compare 10 Hermes memory options across local storage, user modeling, knowledge graphs, self-hosting, and cloud pricing.

entry.title: Shared Long-Term Memory for Claude Code and Codex, Fully Local: A Hindsight Daemon Setup Guide

link.title: Shared Long-Term Memory for Claude Code and Codex, Fully Local: A Hindsight Daemon Setup Guide

entry.content:
This is a start-to-finish guide to giving Claude Code and Codex CLI a shared long-term memory that runs entirely on your Mac. It uses Hindsight, an MIT-licensed agent-memory engine, in local daemon mode. Your ChatGPT plan (model gpt-6-luna) does the memory extraction, the database lives in a folder you choose, and only the repositories you list are ever remembered.

I wrote it as the runbook for setting up a second laptop. Follow the steps in order.

Versions used (Oct 2026): @vectorize-io/hindsight-coding-agents 0.8.2, hindsight-api 1.1.0, hindsight CLI 1.1.0, macOS on Apple Silicon, zsh. Newer releases may differ. See the Coding Agents docs.

What you will have at the end

Claude Code ─┐  hooks: SessionStart · UserPromptSubmit · Stop
             ├─►  Hindsight daemon (hindsight-embed)   http://127.0.0.1:9077
Codex CLI ───┘  MCP server: hindsight_* tools          │
                                                       ├─ embedded PostgreSQL (pg0)
                                                       │    data in ~/projects/hindsight-data
                                                       └─ LLM: chatgpt provider, gpt-6-luna
hindsight CLI ─────────────────────────────────────────┤
hindsight ui (web control plane, http://localhost:9999)┘
  • One plugin for both agents. @vectorize-io/hindsight-coding-agents installs three hooks, an MCP server with the hindsight_* tools, and a companion skill into each agent.
  • One memory bank per repository, named coding-agent::<repo>. Claude Code and Codex read and write the same bank, so a decision made in one is visible in the other.
  • Automatic capture and recall. A session’s first prompt gets a memory synthesis injected. Each session is written back when it ends. Git history and a short codebase survey seed every new bank, and the survey re-runs as the code moves on.
  • Five knowledge pages per repo: Component map, Conventions and patterns, Core concepts, Key decisions and rationale, and Initiatives and enhancements.
  • Opt-in only. Repositories you don’t list are never touched.

Step 1 — Prerequisites

Requirement Why Check / install
Claude Code and/or Codex CLI The agents being wired claude --version, codex --version
Node.js (npx) Runs the plugin installer and the hooks node --version
uv The daemon is launched with uvx brew install uv
Rust toolchain, current Daemon mode on macOS builds a dependency (litellm) that has no macOS wheel rustup update stable
ChatGPT plan that allows usage in third-party apps Pays for memory extraction instead of an API key Confirmed during sign-in (Step 3)
hindsight CLI (recommended) Inspect banks, refresh pages, launch the web UI curl -fsSL https://hindsight.vectorize.io/get-cli \| bash

Step 2 — Write the config file first

Create ~/.hindsight/coding-agent.json before installing, so the first session already follows your rules:

{
  "optInOnly": true,
  "optInPaths": ["~/projects/my-repo"],
  "pageTriggerCron": "H * * * *",
  "surveyRefreshCommits": 20
}

chmod 600 ~/.hindsight/coding-agent.json

What each key does:

  • optInOnly: true: memory is off everywhere by default. A repository outside optInPaths is inert: no bank is created, nothing is retained, and nothing is seeded.
  • optInPaths: path prefixes, with ~ expanded. ~/projects/my-repo approves that repo and its git worktrees. ~/projects would approve every repo under it, each with its own bank. To add a repo later, append its path; there is nothing to reinstall.
  • pageTriggerCron: "H * * * *": refreshes each knowledge page at most once an hour. This is the default; writing it out makes it easy to change. H is replaced by a value hashed from the bank and page name, so pages refresh at different minutes instead of all at once. A refresh is skipped when nothing new arrived. Each refresh is one LLM synthesis per page. With a local daemon that comes out of your ChatGPT plan, so hourly is affordable. Use "H H * * *" (once a day) if you want to save plan usage.
  • surveyRefreshCommits: 20: the codebase survey that seeds a new bank’s structural knowledge re-runs whenever 20 new commits have landed since the last survey. This is the default. In Claude Code each survey is a headless claude -p --model haiku run capped at $2 (surveyModel, surveyBudgetUsd). In Codex it runs through Codex itself. Set it to 0 to survey each repo only once, when it is first opened. Busy repos will otherwise keep re-surveying.

The installer adds "serverMode": "daemon" to this file in Step 5.

On a company laptop: list only repositories you are allowed to process this way. With the daemon, memory stays on disk locally, but the extraction step still sends transcript text to your LLM provider (OpenAI, through your ChatGPT plan). Each laptop also has its own memory. Two daemons don’t sync.

Opt-in list or every repo?

The config file supports two modes. Pick one per machine:

Mode Config When to use it
Opt-in only (allowlist) "optInOnly": true + "optInPaths": [...] A work laptop, or any machine where only some repositories may be processed
Every repo (denylist) Remove optInOnly and optInPaths entirely; exclude individual repos with banks.<id>.disabled A personal machine where you want memory everywhere

Switching from opt-in to every repo means deleting the two keys:

{
  "serverMode": "daemon",
  "pageTriggerCron": "H * * * *",
  "surveyRefreshCommits": 20,
  "banks": {
    "coding-agent::private-notes": { "disabled": true }
  }
}

The change applies at your next prompt, because the hooks re-read the file on every call. MCP tools pick it up in the next session. From then on, the first session in any repo creates its coding-agent::<repo> bank, seeds it from git history (the most recent commits, 300 by default), and runs a codebase survey. The survey runs again every surveyRefreshCommits (20) new commits. In Claude Code each survey is a claude -p --model haiku run with a $2 budget cap. Every repo’s transcripts now go to your extraction LLM. With a local daemon the storage stays on your Mac, but the extraction still happens at the provider. Disable the repos where that is not acceptable.

Optional per-repo controls live in the same file, keyed by bank id:

{
  "banks": {
    "coding-agent::some-repo": { "disabled": true },
    "coding-agent::big-monorepo": { "gitIngest": "full", "retainSessions": false }
  }
}

Step 3 — Sign Hindsight in to your ChatGPT plan

Hindsight’s chatgpt provider uses OpenAI’s official Sign in with ChatGPT flow. Hindsight registers as its own OAuth client and stores its own credentials, separate from the Codex CLI’s login.

uvx --from hindsight-api-slim hindsight-admin chatgpt login

A browser window opens. Sign in and approve plan usage. The command waits for the callback on 127.0.0.1:1455, then saves ~/.hindsight/chatgpt/credentials.json with mode 0600.

You may see warnings that sentence-transformers is not installed. They come from running the admin tool out of the slim package and do not affect sign-in.

Confirm:

uvx --from hindsight-api-slim hindsight-admin chatgpt status
# Signed in: yes
# Plan usage enabled: yes

Tokens refresh automatically. Usage counts against your ChatGPT plan and shows at https://chatgpt.com/settings/usage.

Step 4 — Pin the provider and model in your shell

Add to ~/.zshrc:

# Hindsight daemon: extract memories with the ChatGPT plan, model pinned
export HINDSIGHT_API_LLM_PROVIDER=chatgpt
export HINDSIGHT_API_LLM_MODEL=gpt-6-luna

Open a new terminal and check:

echo "$HINDSIGHT_API_LLM_PROVIDER / $HINDSIGHT_API_LLM_MODEL"
# chatgpt / gpt-6-luna

Why set both explicitly:

  • Provider. When the daemon starts, the plugin chooses the provider in this order: HINDSIGHT_API_LLM_PROVIDER, then whichever of OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, GROQ_API_KEY is set first, then claude-code if the claude CLI is on PATH. Setting it explicitly guarantees chatgpt, even if an API key happens to be in your environment.
  • Model. gpt-6-luna is the chatgpt provider’s default today. Pinning it keeps it if a future release changes the default. The runtime updates itself daily.
  • All HINDSIGHT_API_* variables in the environment that starts the daemon are passed on to it. To use a different model only for extraction, use the per-operation variables (for example HINDSIGHT_API_RETAIN_LLM_MODEL).

Step 5 — Install the plugin in daemon mode

From that new terminal:

npx @vectorize-io/hindsight-coding-agents install claude-code codex --server daemon

The output should include local extraction will use chatgpt (from HINDSIGHT_API_LLM_PROVIDER). The installer:

Agent What gets wired
Claude Code 3 hooks merged into ~/.claude/settings.json; MCP server registered with claude mcp add (user scope); skill at ~/.claude/skills/hindsight-coding-agent
Codex CLI 3 hooks merged into ~/.codex/hooks.json; [mcp_servers.hindsight] in ~/.codex/config.toml; skill at ~/.agents/skills/hindsight-coding-agent
Shared Runtime copied to ~/.hindsight/coding-agents; "serverMode": "daemon" written to ~/.hindsight/coding-agent.json

Codex also needs its hooks feature flag. If ~/.codex/config.toml has no [features] section, the installer adds one for you. If the section already exists, the installer prints a reminder instead, and you add the line yourself:

[features]
hooks = true

The installer accepts either hooks = true or the older spelling codex_hooks = true, which some docs still use.

Notes:

  • The plugin is installed with npx, not through a Claude Code marketplace, so it is not listed under /plugin. Manage it with npx @vectorize-io/hindsight-coding-agents install | uninstall | update | stats.
  • If an older per-agent Hindsight plugin (such as hindsight-memory) is installed, uninstall it first so only one set of hooks runs.

Step 6 — Start the daemon and verify it

The SessionStart and Stop hooks start the daemon by themselves, in the background, whenever port 9077 is free. Start it once by hand so the slow first run (download, Rust build, model load) happens while you watch:

node ~/.hindsight/coding-agents/dist/daemon-start.js --harness claude-code

Verify:

lsof -iTCP:9077 -sTCP:LISTEN                 # a python process on localhost:9077

PID=$(lsof -tiTCP:9077 -sTCP:LISTEN)
ps eww -p $PID | tr ' ' '\n' | grep '^HINDSIGHT_API_LLM_'
# HINDSIGHT_API_LLM_PROVIDER=chatgpt
# HINDSIGHT_API_LLM_MODEL=gpt-6-luna

Under the hood, the plugin asks hindsight-embed to start the server. hindsight-embed runs hindsight-api --idle-timeout 0 --port 9077 together with an embedded PostgreSQL 18 instance managed by pg0.

Step 7 — Pin the provider in the daemon profile file

The daemon also has a per-profile env file, ~/.hindsight/profiles/coding-agent.env, created on first start. Make it agree with your shell. Then a daemon started from a context that doesn’t load ~/.zshrc, such as an agent opened from the Dock, still uses ChatGPT and gpt-6-luna:

f=~/.hindsight/profiles/coding-agent.env
cp "$f" "$f.bak"
grep -n '^HINDSIGHT_API_LLM_' "$f"        # inspect what it currently says

Edit it so it contains these two lines, and remove any HINDSIGHT_API_LLM_API_KEY= line:

HINDSIGHT_API_LLM_PROVIDER=chatgpt
HINDSIGHT_API_LLM_MODEL=gpt-6-luna

chmod 600 "$f" "$f.bak"

Step 8 — Put the memory bank where you want it

By default the database lives in ~/.pg0/instances/hindsight-embed-coding-agent/data. Hindsight has no setting for this path, but pg0 follows a symlink. Here is how to move it to ~/projects/hindsight-data.

  1. Stop the daemon and its PostgreSQL. Never copy a running database.

    kill $(lsof -tiTCP:9077 -sTCP:LISTEN)
# wait until postgres has exited and postmaster.pid is gone
pgrep -f 'postgres -D .*hindsight-embed-coding-agent' || echo "postgres stopped"
ls ~/.pg0/instances/hindsight-embed-coding-agent/data/postmaster.pid 2>/dev/null || echo "clean shutdown"

  2. Copy, verify, then swap in a symlink:

    SRC=~/.pg0/instances/hindsight-embed-coding-agent
DST=~/projects/hindsight-data
mkdir -p "$DST"
cp -a "$SRC" "$DST/"                                       # -a keeps the 0700 permissions PostgreSQL requires
diff -rq "$SRC" "$DST/hindsight-embed-coding-agent" && echo "identical"
mv "$SRC" "$SRC.old"
ln -s "$DST/hindsight-embed-coding-agent" "$SRC"

  3. Restart and confirm PostgreSQL now runs from the new folder:

    node ~/.hindsight/coding-agents/dist/daemon-start.js --harness claude-code
lsof -p $(pgrep -f 'postgres -D .*hindsight-embed-coding-agent' | head -1) | grep -m1 hindsight-data

  4. Once everything works (Step 13), delete $SRC.old.

Keep ~/projects/hindsight-data out of git and out of iCloud Drive or Dropbox. Live syncing can corrupt a running database. To back it up, stop the daemon and copy the folder.

Step 9 — Seed memory from past conversations

From inside each opted-in repository:

cd ~/projects/my-repo
npx @vectorize-io/hindsight-coding-agents install claude-code codex --import-conversations
  • The import reads the agent’s local transcripts and keeps only sessions whose recorded working directory is this repository.
  • It uses LLM tokens in proportion to the history (your ChatGPT plan here). It is safe to re-run, because documents are de-duplicated by id.
  • Git commit messages and a codebase survey are ingested automatically at the next session start. New commits are appended as they land, and the survey re-runs every 20 commits (surveyRefreshCommits).
  • CLAUDE.md and the agents’ own memory notes are not imported. CLAUDE.md is loaded into every session anyway. Step 10 imports the memory notes.

Step 10 — Import the agents’ own memory notes

Transcripts are the raw record. Each agent also keeps a curated memory of what it learned, and the plugin imports neither:

Agent Where its memory lives Shape
Claude Code ~/.claude/projects/<repo path, every non-alphanumeric character as "-">/memory/: a MEMORY.md index of ## sections plus one .md file per note Already one folder per repo
Codex ~/.codex/memories/MEMORY.md, written while generate_memories = true under [memories] in ~/.codex/config.toml One file for all repos. Each # Task Group: lists the cwd= of the sessions it came from

You can ask an agent to copy these in with hindsight_ingest_document, and for a few notes that works. It does not scale. The agent reads every note into its context, then writes the full text back out as tool arguments, and it may paraphrase on the way. It also has no way to tell which notes changed since last time. A script that hands the files straight to the daemon avoids all three problems:

curl -fsSL -o ~/.hindsight/hindsight-sync-memory.py \
  https://kaopu-ai.github.io/assets/scripts/hindsight-sync-memory.py
python3 ~/.hindsight/hindsight-sync-memory.py --check   # list what would change: no LLM calls, no writes
python3 ~/.hindsight/hindsight-sync-memory.py           # retain what changed, delete what is gone, wait for the jobs

The script talks to the daemon through the hindsight CLI, so point the CLI at the daemon first (Step 12). It needs only Python 3’s standard library. Read it before you run it: hindsight-sync-memory.py.

What it does:

  • One document per unit, with a stable id. Each ## section of a Claude Code MEMORY.md becomes claude-memory-<section>. It holds the body of every note the section links to, verbatim, under a short header. Sections of an ARCHIVE.md, if you keep one, become claude-memory-archive-<section> and are labelled as history. Notes that no index links to go into claude-memory-unindexed. Each Codex task group becomes codex-memory-<title>. A re-run overwrites the same document instead of adding a copy.
  • Routes Codex groups by cwd. A group goes to coding-agent::<repo> when one of its cwd= paths contains the repo’s directory name, which covers worktrees inside the repo. A group that touched two repos goes into both banks. Groups from scratch directories that have no bank are skipped and listed.
  • Writes only to banks that already exist. It never creates one, so it follows the opt-in choice you made in Step 2. A Claude Code memory folder is matched to a bank when its name ends with the repo’s directory name. Folders that Claude Code creates for worktree sessions end with the worktree name instead, so they are skipped.
  • Re-retains only what changed. Hindsight stores each document’s content_hash as the SHA-256 of its text. The script hashes the text it would send and skips every document that matches. It adds no dates of its own to the text and passes them as the retain timestamp instead, so an unchanged note never looks changed. A second run straight after the first prints Up to date.
  • Deletes only its own leftovers. When a section or task group disappears, its claude-memory-* or codex-memory-* document is deleted. Conversation, git and survey documents from the plugin are never touched.
  • Leaves the rest of ~/.codex/memories/ alone. raw_memories.md and rollout_summaries/ are close to the transcripts Step 9 already imported. memory_summary.md is a profile that spans all repos, not one repo’s knowledge.

Codex remembers whatever you did in a repo’s directory, including things that are not about the code. Before the first real run, read the --check list. To keep a task group out, add a regex for its title as a line of ~/.hindsight/memory-sync-exclude (case-insensitive; blank lines and # comments are ignored). A group that was already imported is deleted on the next run. The list lives outside the script, so a fresh download of the script still honours it.

The first run retains everything, which on my machine was 74 documents across 3 banks. Extraction goes through your ChatGPT plan, the same as in Step 9. After that, only notes that changed cost anything. Codex rewrites its MEMORY.md as it works, and Claude Code adds notes as you go, so re-run the script now and then. --check makes no LLM calls. For a SessionStart hook that only warns, use --quiet: a --check that prints nothing while everything is up to date.

Step 11 — Start fresh agent sessions

The hooks read ~/.hindsight/coding-agent.json every time they run. The MCP server behind the hindsight_* tools reads it once, when it starts. After installing, start new Claude Code and Codex sessions. In an already-open Claude Code session, run /mcp → hindsight → Reconnect.

In a new session you should see the Hindsight memory banner. The tools the agent can call:

Tool Use
hindsight_search_knowledge_pages / hindsight_read_knowledge_page / hindsight_list_knowledge_pages Look up architecture, conventions, decisions
hindsight_reflect Deep reasoning over all memory (“why is X like this?”)
hindsight_ingest_document Save notes or a document into memory
hindsight_capture_initiative Track a new feature or plan as its own page
hindsight_sync_status / hindsight_diagnose Check ingestion status and configuration

Step 12 — Point the CLI at the daemon

Without configuration the hindsight CLI targets http://localhost:8888. Point it at the daemon:

hindsight configure --api-url http://localhost:9077
chmod 600 ~/.hindsight/config

Useful commands (<bank> is coding-agent::my-repo):

hindsight health                              # Status: healthy · Database: connected
hindsight bank list
hindsight bank stats <bank>                   # nodes, links, documents, pending/failed operations
hindsight document list <bank>
hindsight operation list <bank>               # retain / consolidation / refresh jobs and their status
hindsight mental-model list <bank>            # the knowledge pages
hindsight mental-model refresh <bank> <id>    # refresh one page now
hindsight explore                             # interactive terminal explorer

The plugin also ships a one-shot status report:

node ~/.hindsight/coding-agents/dist/status.js --repo ~/projects/my-repo
# {"bank":"coding-agent::my-repo","gitlogPresent":true,"chatDocs":…,"pagesCount":5,"surveyDocs":4,"synced":true,…}

Querying another repo’s memory (cross-bank)

The hindsight_* MCP tools are bound to the current repo’s bank. None of them takes a bank parameter, so an agent working in repo A can’t use them to ask what was decided in repo B. Use the CLI against the other bank instead:

hindsight bank list                                    # find the bank id
hindsight memory recall 'coding-agent::other-repo' "how do we handle retries on 4xx?" -o json
hindsight memory recall 'coding-agent::other-repo' "deployment steps" -t world,experience -o json
  • Use recall, not reflect, for cross-bank lookups. recall returns the stored memories (facts, experiences, observations) ranked by relevance. reflect synthesizes an answer through the target bank’s reflect_mission and disposition. Coding-agent banks get a debugging-assistant mission, so reflect answers in that bank’s voice instead of showing you what it holds.
  • -t/--fact-type narrows the types (world, experience, observation). Separate several with commas (-t world,experience) or repeat the flag. -o json makes the output easy for an agent to parse.
  • Say where a fact came from. When an agent quotes cross-bank results, it should name the source bank (coding-agent::other-repo) so nobody mistakes it for the current repo’s own memory.

  • To make agents do this automatically, add a line like this to your global ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (and Codex’s AGENTS.md):

    - Cross-repo memory: `hindsight_*` MCP tools only see the current repo's bank. To read another repo's
  memory run `hindsight memory recall 'coding-agent::<repo>' "<question>" -o json` (recall, not reflect —
  reflect applies the target bank's mission) and cite the source bank in the answer.
  • If some of your repos must never inform each other, write that rule next to it. Separate banks keep the data apart, but the agent can still bridge them with this command. The CLI query is the only path across banks, so the rule only has to govern that one command.

Step 13 — Generate the knowledge pages

A new bank’s pages show “No content yet.” until their first hourly slot comes, which can take up to an hour. To build them right away (this only uses your ChatGPT plan):

B=coding-agent::my-repo
for id in $(hindsight mental-model list $B -o json | python3 -c "import sys,json;[print(m['id']) for m in json.load(sys.stdin)['items']]"); do
  hindsight mental-model refresh $B $id
done
hindsight operation list $B          # wait for the refresh_mental_model jobs to finish

From then on, each page refreshes at most once an hour, and only when there is new material.

Step 14 — The web UI

The CLI can launch Hindsight’s web control plane (@vectorize-io/hindsight-control-plane, a Next.js app) against the API URL in your CLI config, which is the daemon. It needs Node.js.

By default it is reachable from your whole network with no login. It binds to 0.0.0.0 and requires no sign-in unless an access key is set. Launch it locked down instead:

KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 16); echo "UI access key: $KEY"
HOSTNAME=127.0.0.1 HINDSIGHT_CP_ACCESS_KEY="$KEY" hindsight ui
  • HOSTNAME=127.0.0.1 binds it to localhost only, so other devices on the network can’t reach it. The startup log then shows Network: http://localhost:9999 instead of 0.0.0.0.
  • HINDSIGHT_CP_ACCESS_KEY turns on the login page. Opening / redirects to /login, and the UI’s API routes return 401 until you enter the key printed above.
  • The line No API key configured (public access) in the log is about the key the UI sends to the daemon (HINDSIGHT_CP_DATAPLANE_API_KEY). The local daemon needs none. That line does not mean the UI itself is open.

Then:

  1. The first run installs the control-plane package through npx, which takes about a minute. When it is ready it prints Local: http://localhost:9999 and Connecting to dataplane at: http://localhost:9077.
  2. Open http://localhost:9999 and sign in with the key. The dashboard lists your banks. Inside a bank you can browse documents, memories, entities and the memory graph, look at the knowledge pages (mental models), check operations, and try recall and reflect queries.

  3. Stop it when you’re done:

    kill $(lsof -tiTCP:9999 -sTCP:LISTEN)

For a quick look without a browser, hindsight explore opens a terminal explorer of the same data.

How it behaves day to day

  • Start: the SessionStart and Stop hooks of Claude Code or Codex start the daemon in the background if port 9077 is free. Both agents and all repos share one daemon.
  • Stop: it does not exit when idle. Closing your agents leaves it running, using roughly 1–1.5 GB of RAM and no LLM usage while idle. It stops on reboot and comes back with the next session. To stop it yourself: kill $(lsof -tiTCP:9077 -sTCP:LISTEN).
  • Changing provider, model or other daemon settings: a running daemon is reused and never restarted, so stop it after any change. The next session (or daemon-start.js) starts it with the new settings.
  • Updates: the plugin checks npm once a day and updates its runtime. Re-run install only when a release adds new hooks.
  • Writes are asynchronous: a saved document appears once its retain job completes (hindsight operation list <bank>).
  • Logs: ~/.hindsight/coding-agents-logs/plugin.log, diag.jsonl (every reflect/retain/page event), usage.jsonl. Summary: npx @vectorize-io/hindsight-coding-agents stats.

Final checklist

  • ~/.zshrc: HINDSIGHT_API_LLM_PROVIDER=chatgpt, HINDSIGHT_API_LLM_MODEL=gpt-6-luna, visible in a new terminal
  • hindsight-admin chatgpt status: signed in, plan usage enabled
  • ~/.hindsight/coding-agent.json: serverMode: "daemon", pageTriggerCron: "H * * * *", surveyRefreshCommits set the way you want (20 by default, 0 = survey once), mode 600. Either optInOnly: true with the right optInPaths, or no opt-in keys plus banks.<id>.disabled for the repos to exclude.
  • Cross-bank lookup works: hindsight memory recall 'coding-agent::<repo>' "<question>" -o json returns results
  • ~/.hindsight/profiles/coding-agent.env: chatgpt + gpt-6-luna, no API-key line, mode 600
  • ~/.codex/config.toml: hooks = true under [features], [mcp_servers.hindsight] present
  • Daemon on 127.0.0.1:9077 with the right HINDSIGHT_API_LLM_* in ps eww; hindsight health healthy
  • ~/.pg0/instances/hindsight-embed-coding-agent → symlink to ~/projects/hindsight-data/…; PostgreSQL has files open there
  • Per repo: status.js --repo … shows synced: true, pagesCount: 5, surveyDocs: 4; hindsight operation list shows nothing failed
  • In a new agent session, hindsight_sync_status returns the same numbers as status.js
  • python3 ~/.hindsight/hindsight-sync-memory.py --check prints Up to date
  • Web UI launched only with HOSTNAME=127.0.0.1 and HINDSIGHT_CP_ACCESS_KEY, and stopped when not in use (nothing listening on :9999)

Uninstall

npx @vectorize-io/hindsight-coding-agents uninstall all     # removes the hooks, MCP entries and skills install added
                                                            # (Codex's [features] hooks flag stays, since other hooks may use it)
kill $(lsof -tiTCP:9077 -sTCP:LISTEN)                       # stop the daemon
# memory data: ~/projects/hindsight-data (and the symlink in ~/.pg0/instances) — delete only if you mean it
entry.summary: Step-by-step: run Hindsight as a local daemon so Claude Code and Codex share per-repo memory, extracted with your ChatGPT plan (gpt-6-luna), with opt-in repos, a custom data folder, and a locked-down web UI.

entry.title: Jev, Drex, and Laya: Three System One Decision Models Compared

link.title: Jev, Drex, and Laya: Three System One Decision Models Compared

entry.content:
A new kind of model showed up in 2026: the System One decision model. Instead of writing an answer token by token, it reads a piece of text (the state) plus a set of typed questions, and returns a probability for each option in a single pass. There is nothing to parse and no free-form output to go wrong.

Three of them are worth knowing about: Jev from TypeSafe, Drex from Nace, and Laya from ConvAI. This post compares them as of October 2026.

One protocol, three models

All three speak the same API: POST /v1/systemone with a state and a map of questions. It is TypeSafe’s API, and Jev was the first model on it; Drex and Laya both ship as wire-compatible replacements, so switching between them is mostly a base-URL change.

They also share the three question types:

Type Asks Returns
choice Pick one of these named options The pick, a confidence, and a distribution
noul Is this proposition true? P(true)
score Where does this sit on an ordered scale? Expected level and a distribution

Typical uses: routing a ticket, classifying an email, checking an extracted field, gating an action behind a guardrail. Code keeps the workflow, permissions, and arithmetic; the model supplies the judgment.

Side by side

  Jev 1.13 (TypeSafe) Drex 2.0 (Nace) Laya (ConvAI)
Weights Closed Open, under Open RAIL-M (use restrictions; not OSI open source) Open, Apache 2.0
Hosted API Yes (api.typesafe.ai; also via OpenRouter) Yes (console.nace.ai) No first-party API; self-host (laya-serve). Third-party: Vercel AI Gateway (free through October 31, 2026, billed after). Plus a demo Space
Model Not disclosed Qwen3.6-35B-A3B MoE (35B total, ~3B active) Encoders: ModernBERT-large 421M, mmBERT-base 322M
Hardware to self-host n/a Large GPU: ~70 GB bf16, ~37 GB Q8 GGUF Small: a T4, or CPU (193–464 ms)
Context 64K per request / 32K per question; 262K with the long-context header 128K state (hosted); self-host defaults to 16K, up to 128K 512 (English) / 1,024; up to 8K multilingual
Latency 236–316 ms p50 (independently measured) ~25 req/s per H100 (vendor) 33–40 ms on a T4 (vendor)
Zero-shot quality The reference point Vendor reports ahead of Jev on its Decision Index (61.25 vs 57.96), slightly behind on JevBench (85.7% vs 86.6%) Weak: 0.362 on typed-decisions, below a 0.461 majority-class baseline
After fine-tuning Not offered; you steer it through state and instructions Offered as a vendor service 0.766 vs a third-party-published Jev 0.727 on the same benchmark
Many options Up to 255; 79.2% on the full Banking77 test (77 labels) Up to 255 Drops past ~20 options at default settings: 0.425 on Banking77
Calibration No vendor figure; independent ECE 0.02–0.35 depending on the task No figures published Over-confident until temperature-fitted (0.466 → 0.081)
Languages English primary; others, including CJK, handled less accurately No list published 100+ (45 of 51 measured languages usable), with a built-in language router
Price $0.042 per 1M input tokens, output free Hosted: $0.06 per 1M input tokens (v2.0), output free, $25 signup credit. Self-host: royalty-free for personal or research use, or organizations under $1M revenue and funding; others need a commercial license Free (self-host)
Rate limits Set per organization in requests/s and tokens/s; the numbers are in your console, not the public docs. My test: ~850 requests/min sustained (806 calls in 57 s, 4 in flight), no 429s Free tier: 120 requests/min, 8 in flight. Paid: 600 requests/min, 16 in flight. My test: 429s on the free tier even when paced below 110 requests/min; none after adding credit (~800 calls in about 2 minutes) None when self-hosted; your own hardware is the limit. AI Gateway limits not published

Jev 1.14 shipped as a preview (jev-preview) on October 14; jev-latest still points to 1.13.

Which one when

  • Jev if you want it to work zero-shot today with the most mature SDKs and docs, and a hosted-only service is fine.
  • Drex if you want both doors open: a hosted API priced close to Jev today, and open weights you can move in-house later if data has to stay in your own environment (check the license if your organization is above its $1M thresholds). It also has the largest default context (128K). Self-hosting it takes a large GPU.
  • Laya if the task is narrow and high-volume, latency matters, and you have labeled examples to fine-tune on. It is the only one that runs comfortably on CPU or at the edge, and the only one that publishes multilingual results.

In one line: Jev is the hosted default, Drex offers the same idea both hosted and as open weights, and Laya is a very small model you train and run yourself.

Read the benchmarks carefully

Almost none of these numbers are directly comparable:

  • Drex’s figures are self-reported by Nace.
  • Laya’s comparisons against Jev use Jev numbers published by third parties; the model card says they were never measured by the Laya team. The widely quoted “beats Jev” result is for a checkpoint fine-tuned on that benchmark’s own training split; the base checkpoint scores below majority-class guessing on it.
  • Jev’s latency, Banking77 and calibration figures come from two independent benchmark repos; TypeSafe itself publishes no accuracy or calibration numbers.

Because the three share a protocol, the honest way to choose is cheap: take 50–100 real decisions from your own workload, run all three, and compare. Each model also has documented weak spots worth testing for: injected text shifting Jev’s probabilities, Laya’s score questions and its noul following option labels instead of the state.

Sources

  • Jev models, context and pricing and API reference
  • Drex, its pricing, limits and rate limits and repo
  • Laya model card and laya-typed-decisions, and Laya on Vercel AI Gateway
  • jev-benchmarks and decision-model-benchmark
